articles.title: Psychologist Adam Grant Shares the No. 1 Habit To Form Deeper Connections With People
articles.summary: Your social habits are crucial for your long-term health. Here’s the simplest way to build deeper social connections, according to psychologist Adam Grant.
articles.body: Your social habits are just as important as eating well and exercising for your long-term health. But many people in the U.S., particularly young adults, feel socially adrift, isolated or lonely. The easiest way to combat loneliness and build deeper social connections with those around you is surprisingly simple — and, ideally, genuinely fun. Expert Tip of the Day: If You Want to Build Deeper Social Connections, Try This If you want to build deeper connections with other people, the best thing to do is simple: Join a club, says Adam Grant, Ph.D., professor at Wharton Business School, organizational psychologist and author of the new book “Vibe: The Secrets of Strong Connections in a Lonely World.” “This is the single most important lifestyle habit we could adopt if we want to strengthen connection,” he tells TODAY.com. “It could be a book club, a gardening group, a painting or pottery experience or a tennis league.” The exact type of club or group you join doesn’t matter — as long as it’s something you enjoy or are interested in doing. “If you get together with people who share your interests,” Grant explains, “it’s a natural opportunity both to build closer connections and have fun while you’re doing it.” Why It Matters In today’s world, many of us are feeling more and more isolated. “Our social networks used to look like spider webs, where everybody in our life knew each other, and now it looks more like we’re the center of a bicycle wheel,” Grant says. “We’re a hub, and we have all these spokes that are disconnected from each other.” That leaves us in a place where we can have individual connections, he explains, but still not have a real sense of community. Social isolation is associated with many negative health effects, especially as we age. Loneliness is linked to increased risks for depression, anxiety, heart attacks, strokes and certain chronic illnesses, the Mayo Clinic says. And even people who seem well-connected on the outside may still feel a sense of loneliness, as TODAY.com explained previously. Joining a group based around a common interest or experience is one way to strengthen your sense of community and feel more seen by those around you. How to Get Started To reap the benefits of a social group, start by thinking about the groups you’re already a part of that you might want to become more involved with. Then, consider your interests and hobbies, as well as your neighborhood and activities. Any of these could be the foundation of a group you could join, such as a new cooking class or walking group in your area. And, previously, TODAY.com recommended meeting with your neighbors, signing up for volunteer work, embarking on a retreat or taking a class focused on a new hobby as great ways to make friends as an adult. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Health insurance scams to watch for during open enrollment
articles.summary: The FTC sent warning letters to 25 companies over misleading health insurance ads as open enrollment brings a surge of deceptive offers online.
articles.body: If you've been shopping for health insurance lately, you've probably noticed the ads popping up everywhere. Some promise surprisingly low monthly payments. Others claim you'll qualify for generous benefits or even receive cash rewards for signing up. And with open enrollment underway, those offers can be awfully tempting. But here's what worries me. You could enroll in what looks like a great health insurance plan, only to discover that it barely covers your medical bills when you actually need care. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is now warning about misleading health insurance advertising, including plans that promise comprehensive coverage but deliver far less. Some offers promote medical discount programs rather than traditional insurance. Others may come from scammers impersonating government agencies or familiar insurance companies. With Americans reviewing their coverage for 2027, knowing how to recognize health insurance scams could save you from a very expensive mistake. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. TRUMP ADMIN CRACKS DOWN ON ESTIMATED $10 BILLION IN OBAMACARE FRAUD, BOOTS MILLIONS FROM ROLLS FTC warns 25 companies about misleading health insurance ads Recently, the FTC announced it was sending warning letters to 25 companies that market healthcare plans or generate sales leads for insurance-related products. The agency identified several advertising practices that could violate federal law. These include misrepresenting a plan's benefits, hiding important costs or falsely suggesting that a limited-benefit product provides comprehensive medical coverage. The FTC also raised concerns about advertisements promising free offers, cash rewards or rebates that people may never receive. Now, there's an important detail here. The FTC says the warning letters do not accuse any of the 25 companies of wrongdoing. Instead, the agency is reminding businesses about advertising laws and warning that it continues to monitor the market. Officials also indicated that additional letters could follow. Still, the timing deserves attention. Open enrollment brings a surge of legitimate advertising from insurance providers. Unfortunately, it also gives dishonest marketers and scammers another opportunity to reach people looking for affordable healthcare. How fake health insurance ads can fool you Let's say you're searching online for a more affordable health insurance plan. You type a few words into Google and see a sponsored result offering excellent coverage at a price that seems almost impossible to beat. The website looks professional. It might display a familiar logo or suggest a connection to a government program. You click through and enter your phone number to learn more. Before long, someone calls with an offer. They tell you that you qualify for special coverage and encourage you to sign up immediately. You may even hear that the deal expires today. Here's where things can get tricky. The website might belong to a lead-generation business collecting information for insurance sellers. Lead generation itself is a legitimate practice, but misleading advertisements can send people toward products they never intended to buy. The FTC warns that scammers sometimes purchase search advertisements that imitate official websites. Some use addresses resembling HealthCare.gov or Medicare.gov. Others copy recognizable branding to create the appearance of legitimacy. We've seen similar tactics with financial scams. CyberGuy previously reported on criminals buying Google ads to steal bank logins. In those cases, sponsored search results directed people to convincing fake banking websites. The same underlying trick can work with health insurance. When an advertisement appears near the top of your search results, it's easy to assume the company behind it has already been checked out. But a paid placement offers no guarantee that the seller or its claims are trustworthy. The cheap health insurance plan that could cost you thousands One of the FTC's biggest concerns involves products that look like comprehensive health insurance but offer limited protection. For example, some advertisements promote medical discount programs. You pay a fee and receive access to discounts from participating healthcare providers. While legitimate discount programs exist, they don't provide the same financial protection as comprehensive insurance. Other products, such as fixed indemnity plans, may pay a predetermined amount when you receive certain medical services. Depending on the policy, that payment could fall far short of your actual bill. Think about what happens if you suddenly need emergency surgery. You might expect your insurance to help cover the expense. Instead, you discover that your plan pays only a limited benefit, leaving you responsible for a substantial portion of the charges. That possibility makes understanding your coverage so important. Plans sold through the official Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace must cover essential health benefits, including emergency services and hospitalization. They also provide coverage for preexisting conditions. However, deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs can still apply. You can review those protections directly through HealthCare.gov's explanation of Marketplace benefits at healthcare.gov/coverage/what-marketplace-plans-cover. Before purchasing any plan, ask exactly what type of coverage you're getting. A low monthly premium means very little if the policy leaves you exposed to major medical expenses. HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS Why health insurance robocalls should raise suspicion Have you ever answered your phone and heard a recorded message claiming you've been approved for an affordable health insurance plan? Maybe the recording tells you that you qualify for special benefits. It might even suggest that you're running out of time to claim them. Be skeptical. The FTC's October 29 consumer warning specifically highlights illegal prerecorded telemarketing calls promoting health insurance. Unsolicited recorded insurance sales calls deserve particular caution. They may come from scammers or businesses using questionable marketing practices. And don't assume a familiar name on your caller ID proves anything. Scammers can manipulate caller ID information to make calls appear to come from legitimate organizations. If you receive an unexpected insurance sales call, hang up. Then contact the insurer through a phone number you've independently verified. Tips to protect yourself from health insurance scams You don't need to become an insurance expert to avoid misleading offers. However, a few simple precautions can help you make a more informed decision before committing to a plan. 1. Start with the official Health Insurance Marketplace The safest starting point for comparing ACA Marketplace coverage is HealthCare.gov. You can also call the Marketplace directly at 1-800-318-2596. If your state operates its own Marketplace, the federal website can direct you there. Avoid starting your search through an unfamiliar advertisement or a link someone sends you unexpectedly. Typing the official website address into your browser gives you greater control over where your information goes. 2. Look carefully at sponsored search results A sponsored result means an advertiser paid for placement. It doesn't mean the government has approved the company or verified every claim in the advertisement. Check the website address before entering personal information. Watch for misspelled domains or websites that imitate official government branding. If something looks suspicious, close the page and navigate directly to the organization you're trying to reach. 3. Ask for the actual insurance benefits in writing Before enrolling, request the plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) when applicable. This document explains important costs and coverage details in a standardized format. Pay particular attention to deductibles and out-of-pocket limits. Check whether your doctors participate in the plan's network. Also, make sure the policy covers the medications or treatments you need. You can learn more about these documents through HealthCare.gov's Summary of Benefits and Coverage guide at healthcare.gov/health-care-law-protections/summary-of-benefits-and-coverage/. 4. Be cautious about promises of free money The FTC specifically warns about misleading offers that promise cash rewards or other incentives for enrolling in healthcare plans. Now, legitimate Marketplace financial assistance does exist. Depending on your eligibility, premium tax credits can reduce what you pay for coverage. However, that assistance follows established eligibility rules. If someone promises guaranteed cash simply for signing up or refuses to explain the terms, take a closer look before providing personal information. 5. Verify the company before you pay If you're considering a plan sold outside the official Marketplace, contact your state's insurance department. Ask whether the company and agent are properly licensed and whether the product provides the coverage being advertised. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners provides resources to help you find your state insurance regulator. Also, be cautious about anyone pressuring you to enroll immediately. Legitimate insurers should provide the information you need to review a policy before purchasing it. FAKE SOCIAL SECURITY STATEMENT EMAIL HIDES A SCAM 6. Protect your personal information Health insurance applications can require sensitive information. That makes fake enrollment websites particularly dangerous. Never provide your Social Security number or banking details to someone who contacts you unexpectedly unless you've independently verified their identity and the reason they need the information. If you're unsure about an offer, contact the insurance company directly. You can also find trained Marketplace enrollment assistance through HealthCare.gov's official help page at healthcare.gov/find-assistance/. 7. Use strong antivirus software Scammers may use fake health insurance websites, phishing emails or text messages to trick you into clicking malicious links. Strong antivirus software can help detect dangerous websites and block malware that could steal your passwords or personal information. Some security tools can also warn you about suspicious links before you open them. While antivirus protection can't tell you whether an insurance policy provides legitimate coverage, it adds another layer of protection when you're shopping online. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. 8. Consider identity theft protection Health insurance scams can expose some of your most sensitive information, including your Social Security number and financial details. An identity theft protection service can monitor for signs that criminals are misusing your information and alert you to suspicious activity. Some services also provide assistance if your identity is stolen. Keep in mind that these services can't prevent every type of fraud. If you've already shared sensitive information with a scammer, visit IdentityTheft.gov to learn what steps to take. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com. 9. Use strong passwords and two-factor authentication If you create an account to compare or manage health insurance coverage, protect it with a strong, unique password. A password manager can help you create and store passwords without reusing them across multiple websites. Also, enable two-factor authentication (2FA) whenever it's available. That extra security step can make it harder for someone to access your account if your password gets stolen. Important health insurance enrollment dates for 2027 If you're reviewing health insurance for next year, knowing the enrollment deadlines can also protect you from misleading sales pitches. According to the current HealthCare.gov enrollment calendar, federal Marketplace open enrollment for 2027 coverage began November 1, 2026, and ends January 15, 2027. However, there's another important deadline. To have your Marketplace coverage begin January 1, 2027, you generally need to enroll by December 15, 2026, and pay your first premium. Enrollments completed from December 16 through January 15 generally begin February 1, provided the first premium is paid. Some state-operated Marketplaces may have different dates, so check your state's official website. Medicare operates on a separate schedule. Its annual open enrollment period runs from October 15 through December 7, 2026, for coverage changes taking effect January 1, 2027. If you're comparing Medicare plans, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). Knowing these dates makes it easier to question someone who calls with a supposedly urgent deadline that doesn't match the official schedule. What to do if you've already responded to a suspicious insurance offer Maybe you've already clicked an advertisement or spoken with someone about a plan that now seems questionable. Perhaps you've even paid an enrollment fee. The first thing I recommend is verifying whether you actually have insurance coverage. Contact the insurance company directly using its official phone number. Ask for confirmation of your policy and request written information explaining your benefits. If you shared financial information with a suspicious seller, contact your bank or credit card company. Explain what happened and ask about protecting your account or disputing unauthorized charges. And if you provided sensitive identifying information to someone you suspect was a scammer, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting yourself. You can also report misleading health insurance advertisements and illegal robocalls to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The sooner you investigate a suspicious transaction or possible identity theft, the more options you may have to limit the damage. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me most about these health insurance offers is how easily someone could believe they're protected when they're actually facing an enormous financial risk. Think about it. You pay your monthly bill, receive something that looks like an insurance card and assume you're covered. Then a medical emergency happens, and suddenly you discover your plan has serious limitations. That's a frightening position to be in, especially when medical expenses can add up so quickly. I also think this FTC warning says something important about how we shop online. We've become accustomed to seeing sponsored results at the top of our searches. But the company willing to pay for that placement may have little to do with the organization we're actually trying to reach. When it comes to health insurance, I would always start with the official Marketplace or a company I've independently verified. And before signing anything, I want to know exactly what happens if I end up in the emergency room. That's the question that can reveal whether a seemingly affordable plan will actually protect you. Should companies face tougher penalties for advertising misleading health benefits, especially when someone's financial security could be at stake? articles.title: AIIMS-like facility is must for Prayagraj: Ujjwal Raman
articles.summary: Allahabad MP Ujjwal Raman Singh urges an AIIMS-like institute for Prayagraj as SRN Hospital adds ventilators and dialysis machines via CWC CSR support.
articles.body: times news networkPrayagraj: Allahabad MP Ujjwal Raman Singh said that an AIIMS-like institution is the need of the hour for Prayagraj as patients travel to Lucknow and Delhi for treatment of chronic diseases.Inaugurating ventilators and dialysis machines installed at Swaroop Rani Nehru Hospital, affiliated to Motilal Nehru Medical College, Singh said: “Prayagraj needs an AIIMS-like institution as patients suffering from chronic diseases have no option but to travel to Lucknow and Delhi for treatment because the city lacks adequate advanced medical infrastructure.”The equipment installed at the hospital has been procured through the corporate social responsibility initiative of the Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC). Under the programme, medical equipment worth Rs 2 crore were provided to Motilal Nehru Medical College, while ventilators worth Rs 2.5 crore have been supplied to SGPGI, Lucknow.Calling the initiative a major step towards improving critical care facilities, Singh said the ventilators and dialysis machines would significantly strengthen treatment options for seriously ill patients and benefit thousands of people in the region.MP’s representative Vinay Kushwaha highlighted the institution’s history, noting that Motilal Nehru Medical College was established in 1961 under then Uttar Pradesh chief minister Chandra Bhanu Gupta.“Former MP Kunwar Rewati Raman Singh played a key role in securing Rs 125 crore from the Union govt during the Manmohan Singh-led UPA regime, while the Akhilesh Yadav govt contributed Rs 25 crore for developing the super-specialty hospital,” he said.Principal Dr AK Verma, CWC HR head Prakash Chandra Rai, chief medical superintendent Dr Neelma Singh, Dr Mohit Jain, Dr Arvind Gupta, Dr Anil Singh, Dr Santosh Maurya and Vinay Kushwaha were present on the occasion.Stay updated with the latest Prayagraj news. articles.title: Woman alleges medical negligence at Chavakkad Taluk Hospital
articles.summary: 21-year-old woman alleges cotton wad left after delivery at Chavakkad Taluk Hospital, Thrissur; doctor denies; health team and police probe underway.
articles.body: Thrissur: A 21-year-old woman has accused healthcare personnel at Chavakkad Taluk Hospital in Thrissur of leaving a cotton wad inside her vaginal canal during post-delivery procedures, causing prolonged pain and suffering. Hospital doctor Ditto Tom denied the allegations.Fathimathul Sharafiya of Kadappuram near Chavakkad alleged that the doctor attributed her pain and discomfort to an infection and prescribed antibiotics without further investigation despite her repeated complaints.Sharafiya said a scan at a private clinic detected the cotton wad, which was removed at another private healthcare facility. She also alleged that the doctor offered compensation to settle the matter. She said she has medical records, including the scan report, to substantiate her allegations.Dr Tom claimed Sharafiya made the allegations because he refused to pay her money. He maintained that he followed prescribed medical protocols during her delivery. He said cotton was placed around the periphery, not inside her body, to check bleeding and was removed within half an hour, with the timings recorded in hospital records.Taluk hospital medical superintendent Dr Shajkumar forwarded the complaint to district medical officer Sujatha M, who said a team of gynaecologists would conduct a preliminary inquiry.Chavakkad Police has recorded statements from Sharafiya and her husband Muhammed Shahir. articles.title: Woman claims hospital injected wrong drug into her spine during knee surgery, leaving her unable to walk
articles.summary: Linda Gilbert's lawsuit alleges Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown injected potassium phosphate instead of mepivacaine, causing incomplete paraplegia.
articles.body: A Nashville woman is seeking $150 million from Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown, alleging that a medication error during knee replacement surgery left her with a permanent spinal cord injury. Linda Gilbert, who was 78 at the time of the incident, alleges that hospital staff injected the wrong drug into her spinal canal during the procedure. A total of four surgery patients received potassium phosphate instead of the intended anesthetic, mepivacaine, on Aug. 14, according to an Aug. 21 statement published on the hospital system’s website. ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS The Nov. 6 complaint, which was provided to Fox News Digital by Gilbert’s attorney, alleges the injection severely injured her spinal cord and nerves, leaving her with incomplete paraplegia, severe weakness in both legs and the inability to walk, drive or live independently. Gilbert also developed shock and respiratory failure requiring a ventilator, according to the filing. The lawsuit alleges that the patient’s injuries are permanent and says she remained in inpatient rehabilitation at a spinal cord injury center in Atlanta at the time it was filed. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Gilbert’s lawsuit claims that staff continued using syringes from the same batch after two earlier patients reported burning pain. It also alleges medication preparation and verification failures, along with delays in treatment. The patient is seeking $50 million in compensatory damages and $100 million in punitive damages. Potassium phosphate is used to treat low phosphorus levels and to supply phosphorus in intravenous nutrition. Its prescribing information specifies that it must be diluted and administered through a vein. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The label warns that excessive doses or overly rapid intravenous administration can cause dangerous heart rhythms, cardiac arrest, seizures and death, according to prescribing information available on NIH’s DailyMed. Those warnings concern intravenous use, rather than injection into the spinal canal as alleged in Gilbert’s lawsuit. "Our hearts remain with the four patients and families impacted by the recent medication error that occurred at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown." In a statement published by local NBC affiliate WSMV on Nov. 9, Ascension Saint Thomas said it was aware of the complaint and was cooperating with the legal process, but could not share additional details because the case was ongoing. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Our hearts remain with the four patients and families impacted by the recent medication error that occurred at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown," the hospital wrote in a Sept. 11 statement on its website. In a Sept. 16 update, the hospital said it was working with an independent quality consultant to "guide and verify the full scope of our corrective actions and process enhancements," adding that it remained "committed to learning from this and upholding the standards of patient safety, quality, and compassionate care." About 790,000 total knee replacements are performed each year in the U.S., according to the American College of Rheumatology. Most patients experience substantial pain relief and improved mobility, with only 2% reporting serious complications, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons states. Fox News Digital reached out to Ascension Saint Thomas, Gilbert’s attorney, the Tennessee Health Facilities Commission and the Institute for Safe Medication Practices for comment.

articles.title: As a Top Sleep Doctor, I Didn’t Think I Could Get Sleep Apnea. What My Own Diagnosis Taught Me
articles.summary: When my at-home sleep test showed my breathing was being interrupted 26 times an hour, I thought something was wrong with the equipment.
articles.body: When my at-home sleep test showed my breathing was being interrupted 26 times an hour, I thought something was wrong with the equipment. After more than 27 years helping people understand their sleep problems, I asked for another test. Same result. The Sleep Doctor, as I’ve come to be known, had moderate obstructive sleep apnea. I was having a difficult time believing it. I knew the symptoms, risk factors, and how easily people could explain away exhaustion. Now it was my turn. At 57, I noticed I had less energy and weaker workouts. Exercise has always been a big part of my life, so I called my doctor. Blood work didn’t explain my sluggishness, so we looked at testosterone. My testosterone wasn’t low, but we tried treatment anyway: six months of an oral form, followed by three months of injections. My energy didn’t improve, but I did lose more hair (which was not exactly the transformation I had in mind). Then my doctor asked: When was the last time I’d had a sleep study? Early in my career, I would regularly test new sleep lab equipment on myself. Absent that routine, I hadn’t repeated testing, and it had been three years since my last test. I arranged an at-home test through SleepDoctor.com, the sleep care company I founded. I wore the device on my wrist for one night in my own bed and assumed I’d cross apnea off the list. I got my answer. It just wasn’t the one I was expecting. I wasn’t overweight. I took care of myself. I didn’t wake up gasping. My wife occasionally mentioned heavy breathing or snoring, especially after alcohol, but I wasn’t the dramatic snorer I associated with apnea. I’d never tell a patient that those things ruled out sleep apnea. Yet somehow, I’d told myself exactly that. The second test showed almost identical results that made it clear: I did in fact have sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea happens when the airway repeatedly narrows or closes during sleep. Your brain briefly awakens you enough to restore your breathing. This disrupts your sleep, often without your remembering it. You get what looks like a full night’s sleep on paper, but these repeated interruptions rob you of the restorative rest you need. Weight can be a contributor, as can age and anatomy. But sometimes the only clue is fatigue. I’d spent months looking everywhere but my sleep for an explanation. I’m far from alone. A new survey of 2,505 people (including people living with sleep apnea, their bed partners and clinicians) found that 1 in 3 U.S. adults living with sleep apnea snored for five or more years before being diagnosed, and only 1 in 5 of them suspected it was “more than snoring.” Looking back, it made me think about a patient I’ll call Ed. He worked for the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, was falling asleep at his desk, and could no longer go on stakeouts. He’d gained weight, felt depressed, and was struggling in his marriage. Testing showed apnea, and we started treatment. At his one-month follow-up, his wife hugged me and said, “Thank you for giving me my husband back.” She handed me the divorce papers she no longer wanted. Patients often tell me, “Dr. Breus, you changed my life.” I think, “You changed your life. I helped you change your sleep.” Getting better sleep means spending less energy just getting through the day and more on the people and things that matter most. Now it was my turn. I started with treatment. A CPAP machine, which uses a mask to deliver a steady stream of air to keep the airway open during sleep, can be a first step. I’d spent years explaining how it works and had even worn one to understand my patients’ experience. But there’s a difference between knowing how a treatment works and living with it. Fortunately, my household offered an unusual incentive. Our two French bulldogs sleep in our bed. One settles between our pillows, head toward my wife, rear end toward me. My wife gets gentle snoring, like a purring kitten. I get the other end of the bulldog. If you know French bulldogs, you understand the appeal of a treatment that offered clean, humidified, filtered air. After nine months, I now use CPAP at home and an oral appliance when I’m traveling, a custom device that moves the lower jaw forward to help keep the airway open. Having both options has made things much easier. My energy has improved. My heart rate variability, which measures variation in time between heartbeats and increases as your body becomes more adaptable, has risen from roughly 17–20 to 35–40, without adding any exercise. For me, that was huge. It’s not proof that it was caused by treatment alone, nor is it a promise of results for anyone else, but alongside better energy, it gave me something concrete to notice. Your treatment depends on your diagnosis and needs, so it’s important to discuss options with your care team. I understood this professionally. Now I appreciate it personally: Treatment must fit the person’s life. I now have a better understanding of the patient who fears a sleep test. A diagnosis can bring both relief and uncertainty — you finally have an explanation, but you also have to figure out what comes next. Accepting a diagnosis doesn’t mean immediately loving treatment. I’ve recommended these treatments for years and still had challenges adjusting. That doesn’t make me a failure as a patient; I just needed a workable routine to help me stay consistent. And that adjustment can be a real hurdle. The same survey found that 52% of diagnosed, untreated adults living with obstructive sleep apnea stopped being consistent with treatment in the first six months, and 56% of diagnosed, untreated adults said dealing with treatment can feel as hard as dealing with sleep apnea itself. If your energy changes, you consistently wake up tired, or someone notices snoring or pauses in breathing, talk to your doctor. Ask whether you should be evaluated for apnea and whether an at-home test is appropriate. Healthy habits, like a consistent wake-up time, morning light, regular movement, and being thoughtful about caffeine and alcohol, hadn’t made me immune to an airway problem. I still recommend them wholeheartedly, but they couldn’t fix what was happening while I slept. My sleep habits weren’t the problem. My breathing was. Now CPAP has a place in my nightly routine, alongside my wife and two bulldogs. I’m waking up with the energy I’d been missing, and a new appreciation for what it means to be on the other side of the diagnosis. I’ve spent decades saying, “Change your sleep, change your life.” Turns out, that applies to the Sleep Doctor, too.

articles.title: Kate Middleton Opens up About Her Cancer Recovery In Rare Interview
articles.summary: Nearly two years after announcing she was in remission from cancer, Catherine, Princess of Wales, is sharing new details about her health journey.
articles.body: Nearly two years after announcing she was in remission from cancer, Catherine, Princess of Wales, is sharing new details about her health journey. The former Kate Middleton sat down with Country Life for an interview featured in the latest edition of the magazine, which her husband, Prince William, guest edited. During the interview, centered on her love for the natural world, Kate compared her recovery journey to nature. “I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time. This is the same in nature. It shows us that periods of rest, reflection and renewal are equally as important as moments of growth,” she said. Kate first revealed her cancer diagnosis in March 2024 and said she was in the process of receiving chemotherapy. She shared that she was in remission in January 2025. Buckingham Palace has not disclosed what kind of cancer the princess was diagnosed with. The British royal said being outdoors played an important role in her recovery. “It is definitely connected, it is about listening and paying attention. What I feel really passionate about, having had first-hand experience, is approaching illness and recovery through a whole-person approach. Yes, serious illness creates a lot of physical challenges, but there is also a deeper part to all of us,” she said. The mother of three said nature has allowed her to find a “deeper connection” to her “mind, body and spirit.” “I think that’s because nature offers something unique. It doesn’t ask anything of us. It doesn’t judge us or expect us to perform. It simply allows us to be. It really has been my sanctuary and a place I’ve instinctively wanted to go,” she said. Asked to weigh in on the therapeutic benefits of nature in health care, the Princess of Wales noted that it’s “interesting” to see science “back up what we instinctively know and feel.” In July 2026, Kate revealed that she completed the National Three Peaks Challenge, which involves summiting the three highest peaks of Scotland, England and Wales in 24 hours. She said on social media at the time the endurance feat was “a chance to explore life beyond diagnosis and to give something back.” “Humans have always turned to nature. Whether it is the beach for healing and recovery, the countryside for peace and perspective or the mountains to find solitude, people have long sought comfort in the natural world. It is such a restorative environment and incorporating nature into someone’s recovery pathway is vital,” she told Country Life. Kate also compared the dynamic state of nature to our ever-changing bodies. “If you look at the natural world, it is hardly ever stagnant; if it is, it’s rarely healthy,” she said. “This has really helped me, thinking about how flow and movement can shift something inside you, whether in your body or your mind or your thoughts.”

articles.title: Woman, 32, Recalls Early Signs of Colorectal Cancer Doctors Dismissed: ‘I Was Sent Home With Tylenol’
articles.summary: Alondra Gibson, a fitness coach, began dealing with abdominal pain and changes in her bowel habits. The next year she was diagnosed with colorectal cancer.
articles.body: When 32-year-old Alondra Gibson first started experiencing persistent abdominal pain and changes in her bowel habits last year, she chalked it up to stress. “In 2025, I was going through a lot of different changes,” Gibson tells TODAY.com. So when she noticed these symptoms, she wasn’t too concerned — and never suspected anything serious. Gibson, who’s based in New York and Dallas, was also the healthiest she’d ever been. She was exercising daily and working as a certified fitness coach, yoga teacher and nutritionist. Persistent Abdominal Pain and Diarrhea In October 2025, Gibson had just returned from a trip to Indonesia when her abdominal pain and diarrhea became more severe. Initially, she assumed it was from routine changes. “I was traveling; I hadn’t been eating consistently,” says Gibson. When the pain worsened after a kettlebell workout class, she suspected the issue was muscular. Gibson also thought her menstrual cycle could be playing a role. “I normally get diarrhea before and after my period, so I thought maybe I’m going through hormonal changes,” she says. In the months that followed, Gibson tried to get back to her normal routine. “The symptoms persisted all the way into 2026. So on January 1, I went to urgent care and told them I was having bad abdominal pains and consistent diarrhea,” she says. Gibson was told to go to the emergency room for testing. There, she had an ultrasound, which came back clear. “I was sent home with Tylenol and told to see a GI doctor,” says Gibson. Symptoms Mistaken for Pelvic Muscle Strain Gibson’s gastroenterologist ordered a plethora of labs to rule out possible diagnoses. “My stool test did come back positive for a stomach virus, but within a few days I should’ve been clear,” she says. However, Gibson’s abdominal pain and diarrhea persisted. And tests for other gastrointestinal disorders came back negative. “One of the things that we thought it could be was a pelvic floor muscle strain. So I started going to pelvic floor therapy, and I went for probably four to six weeks, but things were not changing,” says Gibson. Eventually, the pain became so severe that she was unable to exercise at all. “I could not continue with my normal life. I couldn’t even work.” After a Clear CT Scan, Colonoscopy Reveals Two Tumors Gibson eventually got a CT scan. According to the radiology report, the scan was clear. “I’m very in tune with my body. So I was like, ‘Okay, no, there has to be something wrong,’” she explains. Gibson finally asked her doctor to order a colonoscopy. “It revealed that I had two tumors that were almost completely obstructing my colon,” she says. The tumors were missed on her CT scan nearly two months earlier. “I spent those six to eight weeks in a lot of discomfort,” she recalls. Gibson says her gastroenterologist was just as confused. “He was like, ‘How was this missed? Because it was very much visible in the CT scan,’ And he reached out to the radiology team to change the report, but he took complete ownership,” she says. Then, her doctor told her that it was probably cancer. “I completely blanked out. I was in shock, because I was probably in the best shape of my life then.” Stage 3 Colorectal Cancer Immediately after her colonoscopy, Gibson was scheduled for surgery to remove the tumors and a foot-long section of her colon. Biopsies revealed she had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of colorectal cancer. The tumors had been sitting next to her liver, which was partly covered in cysts, suggesting metastasis. “At that point, it was a 90% chance that I had a Stage 4 colon cancer,” says Gibson. Six weeks after her colon resection, Gibson had surgery to remove part of her liver. Surprisingly, the biopsies were clear. “To this day, we have no idea what happened to that part of my liver,” she says. Gibson was staged down to Stage 3 colon cancer, which has a higher survival rate compared to Stage 4. Chemotherapy and Remission After her colon and liver surgeries, Gibson underwent six months of intensive chemotherapy. Due to the risk that it could cause infertility, she froze her eggs right before treatment. Gibson celebrated her 32nd birthday while receiving an infusion of FOLFOX, a chemotherapy regimen, delivered through a port in her chest. “I was a zombie. I was sleeping the entire time. I didn’t have much (of an) appetite. I had intense fatigue and then a lot of hair thinning, so I had to cut my hair,” Gibson says. Gibson finished her last round of chemotherapy this September. “I had multiple scans, and everything came back clear. I was able to ring the bell in October,” she says. Currently, Gibson is in remission with no evidence of disease, which means that there is no detectable cancer in her body. “For the next three years, I’ll be getting regular CT scans every three months, then I’ll also be doing blood tests which look for proteins from the cancer,” says Gibson. Recently, the 32-year-old has been able to start working out again, with the encouragement of her husband. “I like to move my body, so for me, that was very important,” says Gibson. Exercise has also helped with her peripheral neuropathy, or numbness in the toes and fingers, which can result from chemotherapy. Although she hasn’t been able to return to her full routine or coaching yet, Gibson is getting stronger every day. “I’m actually training for the New York City Half Marathon this upcoming March,” she says. Colorectal Cancer Rates Rising in Young Adults A recent study in NEJM Evidence shows that colorectal cancer rates are rising among all age groups in the U.S., contributing to an increase in the overall incidence for the first time in over two decades. Young people are being hit especially hard. Between 2013 and 2022, colorectal cancer rates climbed 3% every year among adults ages 20 to 49, per American Cancer Society statistics. Many of these young patients, like Gibson, were diagnosed before they qualified for routine screening. The ACS recommends adults at average risk start getting colonoscopies at age 45. In addition to being young and otherwise healthy, Gibson had no risk factors for colorectal cancer. “I did genetic testing, and it was not genetic. I don’t have anyone in my family who has ever had colon cancer or cancer in general,” she says. What led to Gibson’s diagnosis was her relentless pursuit of answers to explain her unusual symptoms — a pattern she’s observed among other young patients. Gibson uses CancerBuddy, a non-profit peer support app to connect cancer patients and survivors. “I started to understand, through our group chat, that you can have so many different symptoms. People think it’s always blood in the stool, but it isn’t just one specific thing; it really varies,” says Gibson. Recalling the day she learned she had cancer, Gibson says an unexpected feeling came over her. “I remember, I was almost in relief. I know that sounds crazy,” she says. “I was just happy that we understood what was happening because I knew that there was something wrong.”

articles.title: New weight-loss drug wipes out chronic knee pain in some patients, researchers say
articles.summary: Northwestern University-led trials found retatrutide helped two-thirds of obese knee osteoarthritis patients cut pain by half in late-stage studies.
articles.body: An experimental weight-loss drug significantly reduced chronic knee pain and improved mobility in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis, according to two clinical trials led by researchers at Northwestern University. The trials, which were funded by Eli Lilly and published in The New England Journal of Medicine, evaluated retatrutide, a once-weekly injectable medication developed by Eli Lilly and Co. Retatrutide, which is not yet FDA-approved, mimics three hormones involved in appetite and metabolism — GLP-1, GIP and glucagon — and has produced substantial weight loss in clinical trials. WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF The late-stage trials enrolled more than 1,000 adults who were overweight or obese, did not have diabetes, and experienced painful knee osteoarthritis. After 68 weeks in one trial and 80 weeks in the other, participants receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost about a quarter of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that roughly two-thirds of those treated with the drug achieved at least a 50% drop in knee pain, compared with 38% of those receiving a placebo. Painful knee osteoarthritis affects an estimated 15 million Americans. Beyond pain relief and functional gains, participants experienced reductions in blood pressure, lower blood lipid levels and decreased systemic inflammation, according to the researchers. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common side effects, and serious adverse events were more common among participants receiving retatrutide than among those receiving placebo. KNEE TREATMENT WITHOUT SURGERY OFFERS LASTING PAIN RELIEF FOR 80% OF ARTHRITIS PATIENTS, STUDY FINDS Dr. Thomas J. Schnitzer, a professor at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and lead author of the study, said the findings offer therapeutic potential for specific groups of patients. "For people who are obese, not diabetic, have radiographically confirmed knee osteoarthritis that has not progressed to bone on bone, and have consistent moderate knee pain, retatrutide treatment has the potential to result in a significant and meaningful reduction in their knee pain and improvement in their physical function while providing cardiometabolic benefit," Schnitzer told Fox News Digital. While researchers anticipated benefits from the weight reduction, the "complete relief of knee pain" in one of every eight patients taking the drug was a surprise, Schnitzer said. Painful knee osteoarthritis affects an estimated 15 million Americans, often turning routine activities such as standing, walking and climbing stairs into painful challenges. YOUR FAVORITE SNACKS COULD BE QUIETLY WRECKING YOUR KNEES, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS Conventional treatments include physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications and steroid injections, which often offer only limited or temporary relief, according to the researchers. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES While earlier research has found that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can ease knee osteoarthritis symptoms, losing more than 10% through those measures alone can be difficult, particularly when knee pain limits exercise, Schnitzer said. Despite the study's promising outcomes, Schnitzer stressed that there were some limitations. "People with knee OA who were not overweight or obese were not studied, and individuals who were obese and had more advanced OA were also excluded, so we have no information on them," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The trials excluded patients who needed knee replacement surgery. Whether retatrutide slows osteoarthritis progression or reduces the need for future joint replacements remains unknown. For individuals experiencing joint pain who may meet the study criteria, Schnitzer recommended discussing options with a healthcare provider. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If someone fits the profile noted above, and they have been unsuccessful at losing weight, they should speak to their physician about the possibility of being treated with a medication that would help them lose weight, as that could also reduce their knee pain as well as provide cardiometabolic benefits," Schnitzer said. At the same time, he emphasized that medication should not replace healthy daily habits. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Before starting pharmacologic treatment for knee pain, people who are overweight should try diet and exercise and consider interventions such as physical therapy," Schnitzer advised. "Also, even for people on weight-loss medications, exercise is an important part of any treatment plan to maintain as much muscle as possible."

articles.title: Death reported in E coli outbreak linked to California pumpkin patch as more cases emerge
articles.summary: An E. coli outbreak linked to California’s Brookshire Farms has left one person dead, five confirmed infections and 10 suspected cases.
articles.body: One person has died in an E. coli outbreak linked to a California pumpkin farm, San Luis Obispo County health officials confirmed Tuesday. Officials have not released the person’s age or identity. The death follows confirmation of five cases of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection, potentially originating from Brookshire Farms in San Luis Obispo, according to an advisory issued by the County of San Luis Obispo Public Health Department. "We can confirm that one individual associated with the E. coli outbreak has died. We are sharing this information with the permission of the individual’s family," Tom Cuddy, public information officer for the department, said in a statement to The Tribune of San Luis Obispo on Nov. 10. E. COLI OUTBREAK LANDS 3 IN HOSPITAL; HEALTH OFFICIALS INVESTIGATE LINK TO PUMPKIN PATCH "This is truly a heartbreaking development, and our thoughts are with the family and everyone affected by this outbreak. The entire team at Public Health extends our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones during this difficult time." In a Nov. 6 statement, the health department said an additional 10 individuals who visited the farm between Oct. 16 and Oct. 26 and developed symptoms have been deemed "suspect cases." Tests of water, food and other samples from the farm found some bacteria, including other E. coli strains, but did not detect the strain responsible for the outbreak, officials said. People who became ill shared possible exposures to corn cups, pumpkins, hay and water not intended for drinking, but officials could not pinpoint the source. FDA WIDENS CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK INVESTIGATION TO SIX MORE STATES AS CONFIRMED CASES TOP 6,000 No farm animals or petting zoos, which are known to be common sources of this type of infection, were accessible to visitors or operating at the farm. Investigators faced several limitations, including numerous possible sources, items no longer available for testing and delays between exposure and sampling. No further environmental testing is planned, according to the report. "Based on the findings of our investigation, we believe the risk of additional exposure associated with this incident has passed, and there is no longer an ongoing public health threat," said County Health Officer Dr. Christy Mulkerin. "Our hearts go out to the families affected by this outbreak. We thank all those who have helped protect our community in response to this outbreak, and we encourage community members to continue practicing good handwashing and food safety to protect themselves and their families." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Typical symptoms of E. coli include cramping, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea and signs of dehydration, which usually begin within three to 10 days of exposure. Young children under 10 are typically at the highest risk for complications, which can include hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious condition that damages blood cells and can lead to kidney failure, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious disease physician and founder of Wellness Equity Alliance in California, warned that diarrhea can lead to dehydration and fatigue. "The diarrhea is really the key component here, and the stomach cramps," he told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Evans said younger children and older adults can be particularly vulnerable, emphasizing the need to closely watch children younger than 5. Speaking generally about potential exposure routes in pumpkin patches, Evans said E. coli can spread when bacteria from feces reach someone’s mouth. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ He pointed to potentially contaminated food or water, animal contact and person-to-person transmission as possible transmission routes. Evans also noted that not all E. coli bacteria cause illness. The confirmed cases in this investigation involve Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. The health department shared the following safe practices to protect against these types of infections. articles.title: How measles surged in the U.S.
articles.summary: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter.
articles.body: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter. The measles outbreaks across the country have gotten so bad that the U.S. may be removed from a list of countries that have eliminated measles. An NBC News project digs into how that happened. articles.title: What happens to the brain after years of breathing polluted air? Doctors explain the concerns around inflammation, memory and stroke
articles.summary: Ask most people what dirty air does to the body and they’ll talk about the lungs: the cough, the wheeze, the asthma flare-ups.
articles.body: Ask most people what dirty air does to the body and they’ll talk about the lungs: the cough, the wheeze, the asthma flare-ups. Doctors say the brain deserves a place in that conversation too. It runs on a constant supply of oxygen-rich blood, and long-term exposure to polluted air can interfere with that.Particles from vehicles, factories, construction sites and burning waste get into the body with every breath. Once they’re in, they can set off inflammation that doesn’t stay put. Researchers are still working out the long-term neurological effects, but the evidence so far has been enough to raise concern about memory, focus and overall brain health.Dr Aparna Gupta, Director of Neurology at ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, says the topic needs more attention than it gets.How polluted air reaches the brain“Clean, oxygen-rich blood is important for the brain as well, and exposure to polluted air over the long term can have an impact on brain health,” said Dr Gupta.The air we breathe in a polluted city carries fine particles and toxic gases from smoke, exhaust, industrial emissions and dust. The smallest particles travel deep into the lungs and cause inflammation that can spread through the body. From there it can reach the blood vessels, and potentially the brain. Because the brain depends so heavily on healthy circulation, repeated exposure could put its cells under extra strain.Headaches, poor focus and memory lapsesIf you’ve struggled to concentrate or had more headaches than usual on the worst air-quality days, it’s worth noticing. That doesn’t mean pollution is the cause, but it’s not something to wave away either.“Excessive exposure to air pollution has been linked to issues like headaches, diminished concentration and memory issues,” Dr Gupta said.Scientists are also looking at whether long-term exposure is tied to stroke and to conditions that affect memory and thinking. The picture is far from simple, though. Breathing polluted air doesn’t mean someone will develop these conditions, since health and environmental factors all play a part.Who is more at riskNot everyone is affected equally. Children, older adults, and people who already have neurological or heart conditions are more vulnerable. A child’s brain is still developing, an older brain is ageing, and in people with existing illness the body has less room to absorb one more stressor.What about epilepsy?Epilepsy involves abnormal electrical activity in the brain that leads to repeated seizures. Air pollution isn’t regarded as a direct cause of epilepsy, nor as an established seizure trigger.Still, bad air can make breathing harder, disrupt sleep and leave people feeling physically run down. For someone whose seizures are set off by lack of sleep, physical stress or illness, that can matter.“For people who have epilepsy, it is particularly important that they take their medicines regularly and do not forget to take them,” Dr Gupta advised.Patients should keep an eye on any change in their usual seizure pattern, and should never adjust or stop their medication without talking to their neurologist first.Cutting down your exposureThe simplest step is to spend less time in the bad air. When quality is very poor, skip unnecessary outdoor trips, and avoid hard exercise near busy roads. Keeping indoor air as clean as you reasonably can helps too, and it’s sensible to follow local air-quality advisories, especially if you have an existing health condition.For people with epilepsy, Dr Gupta also recommends keeping a regular sleep schedule, staying hydrated, taking medicines on time and avoiding known triggers.Pollution isn’t only a lung problem. Its effects can reach the whole body, brain included, which is a good reason to pay attention to the air you breathe every day.

articles.title: Rainha da Maisena: grávida aumenta amido para tratar glicogenose | G1
articles.standfirst: Letícia Ramos, de Uberaba, no Triângulo Mineiro convive com a glicogenose desde os 2 anos e meio. No início da gestação, ela precisou aumentar a quantidade de amido de milho para evitar episódios de hipoglicemia enquanto aguarda a chegada do primeiro filho, Pedro Luigi.
articles.summary: Com glicogenose, Letícia Ramos aumentou o consumo de amido de milho para 500g diários no início da gestação para evitar hipoglicemia e garantir a saúde do bebê.
articles.body:
**VOU INSERIR VÍDEO AUTOMÁTICO APÓS EDIÇÃO**

A rotina de Letícia Ramos, conhecida nas redes sociais como a 'Rainha da Maisena' , ganhou um novo ingrediente: a maternidade. Aos 35 anos, a moradora de Uberaba , no Triângulo Mineiro, convive desde a infância com uma doença genética rara que a faz consumir amido de milho diariamente.

Grávida do primeiro filho, ela precisou adaptar o tratamento para passar pela gestação com segurança. Em meio à expectativa pela chegada de Pedro Luigi, a quantidade diária de maisena também precisou aumentar.

Diagnosticada com glicogenose tipo 9C aos 2 anos e meio, Letícia precisa consumir amido de milho dissolvido em água em intervalos regulares para manter os níveis de glicose no sangue.

Antes da gravidez, Letícia havia conseguido reduzir a quantidade de amido de milho consumida diariamente após encontrar um tratamento especializado. Com a gestação, porém, o metabolismo mudou, e ela precisou aumentar o consumo novamente.

"Eu estava indo bem com a quantidade de amido de milho, mas, com a gravidez, tive que aumentar um pouquinho. O metabolismo da mulher muda muito nesse período, então é preciso bastante suporte da maisena", disse.

Letícia Ramos, a 'Rainha da Maisena' — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

As mudanças foram mais intensas nas primeiras semanas da gestação. Sem saber que estava grávida, Letícia começou a apresentar alterações no organismo e episódios frequentes de hipoglicemia (queda dos níveis de glicose no sangue). O aumento do fígado, identificado durante exames, também chamou a atenção dos médicos. A gravidez foi descoberta durante a investigação dos sintomas.

Naquele período, Letícia chegou a consumir aproximadamente 500 gramas de amido de milho por dia, o equivalente a 15 quilos por mês. A orientação médica era ingerir 70 gramas a cada três horas, com ajustes conforme os episódios de hipoglicemia.

"Eu tive muita hipoglicemia no começo da gestação. Quando descobri, tentamos controlar o máximo possível. Colocamos o consumo de três em três horas, dependendo de como eu estava. Cheguei a consumir quase meio quilo de maisena por dia", explicou.

Com o acompanhamento de uma equipe multidisciplinar, formada por mais de seis médicos de diferentes cidades, Letícia conseguiu estabilizar o quadro de saúde e reduzir novamente o consumo de amido de milho. Atualmente, ela ingere cerca de nove quilos por mês.

"Agora conseguimos diminuir, graças a Deus. No começo foi mais complicado, mas estamos com uma equipe grande, todo mundo se ajudando para que essa gestação dê certo", disse.

A descoberta da gravidez trouxe alegria, mas também dúvidas e preocupações para Letícia. Ser mãe era um sonho, mas, durante muito tempo, ela acreditou que não conseguiria realizá-lo por causa da glicogenose.

"Eu queria ficar feliz, porque a maioria das mulheres sonha em ser mãe e eu também tinha muito esse sonho. Só que, na minha cabeça, era uma coisa que não existiria. A maioria das meninas que têm glicogenose também tem muito medo de engravidar", afirmou.

A gravidez não foi planejada e, por isso, a descoberta trouxe ainda mais dúvidas e preocupações. Segundo Letícia, antes de engravidar, seria importante realizar exames genéticos para avaliar o risco de transmitir a doença ao bebê.

"Quando descobri, entrei em pânico. Queria estar feliz, mas, ao mesmo tempo, pensava: 'E agora? O que vai acontecer comigo? O que vai acontecer com o bebê? Será que vai dar certo?'", lembrou.

Preocupada, Letícia procurou os médicos que já acompanhavam seu tratamento e conheciam seu histórico de saúde. Aos poucos, uma equipe de especialistas foi formada, com profissionais de Uberaba, São Paulo e Porto Alegre. Ela também passou a receber acompanhamento no Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein.

A equipe acompanha a evolução da gravidez e as adaptações necessárias no tratamento. Segundo Letícia, os primeiros meses foram emocionalmente difíceis. Só no quinto mês ela conseguiu respirar mais aliviada e aproveitar a gestação.

"Agora, no quinto mês, posso dizer que estou respirando, que estou vivendo o momento da gestação. Nos primeiros meses foram momentos tensos e difíceis", afirmou.

'A Rainha da Maisena' agora tem um herdeiro

Letícia, o marido Pedro Mário e a cachorra blackout — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A gravidez também representa uma nova etapa para quem passou boa parte da infância tentando esconder a própria condição. Na primeira entrevista ao g1 , em 2022, Letícia contou que tinha vergonha de consumir amido de milho na frente de outras crianças e chegou a se esconder para tomar a mistura.

Anos depois, transformou justamente essa particularidade em uma forma de acolher outras pessoas. Nas redes sociais, passou a mostrar a rotina com a doença, conquistou milhares de seguidores e ficou conhecida como 'Rainha da maisena'.

Agora, quatro anos depois, a notícia da gestação também repercutiu entre pessoas que convivem com a glicogenose e familiares de crianças diagnosticadas com a condição. Letícia contou que demorou um pouco para compartilhar a novidade, mas decidiu tornar pública a experiência por acreditar que ela pode representar esperança para outras mulheres.

"Muita gente ficou surpresa, principalmente quem tem glicogenose e as mães de crianças que têm a doença. É uma coisa que dá esperança. Eu quero ajudar, responder às perguntas e motivar essas meninas a viverem esse momento", disse.

Apesar da vontade de tranquilizar outras mulheres, ela admite que ainda sente medo e que a responsabilidade de compartilhar uma experiência tão diferente é grande.

"Eu quero que elas vivam esse momento com menos ansiedade do que eu. Acredito que sou uma das primeiras que o pessoal conhece passando por isso, então está todo mundo apostando em mim. Mas também tenho muito medo".

Uma das dúvidas mais frequentes dos seguidores é se Pedro Luigi pode nascer com a mesma doença da mãe. Como a glicogenose é genética, existe essa possibilidade, mas, segundo Letícia, os médicos consideram que as chances são baixas.

Ela explicou que, para a condição se manifestar, é necessário que pai e mãe apresentem alterações genéticas relacionadas à doença. Como o casal não realizou o exame genético antes da gravidez, não foi possível estabelecer uma probabilidade individual.

Casada com o marido Pedro Mario Faquinelli há mais de sete anos, Letícia também encontrou apoio para enfrentar os desafios da gestação. Segundo ela, o marido precisou conhecer melhor a glicogenose no início do relacionamento, mas hoje participa ativamente dos cuidados.

É ele quem ajuda a preparar e entregar as doses de amido de milho nos horários corretos, para que a rotina de tratamento não seja interrompida.

"Ele é meu companheiro até debaixo d'água. Me ajuda muito, cuida muito de mim. É ele quem me dá as doses de amido de milho para eu não perder os horários", contou.

Agora, os dois se preparam para receber Pedro Luigi. O nome do bebê, inclusive, tem uma história divertida: apaixonado por videogames, o casal escolheu uma combinação inspirada nos personagens Mario e Luigi, da Nintendo. Como o pai se chama Pedro Mário, o menino ganhou o nome de Pedro Luigi.

E, se depender de Letícia, o filho terá uma mãe presente em cada etapa da vida, independentemente dos desafios que possam surgir.

"Quero dar muito suporte mental para ele, acolher em todas as decisões e em qualquer coisa que acontecer. Quero ser aquela mãe amiga, que está por dentro de tudo. Quero ser a maior companheira dele para tudo", afirmou.

Para quem transformou uma condição rara em uma forma de inspirar milhares de pessoas, a chegada do primeiro filho abriu um capítulo inédito. E a 'Rainha da Maisena' já tem um pequeno parceiro para dividir as próximas aventuras.

"Quero que as pessoas me vejam como inspiração para ter uma vida normal, leve, cheia de sonhos, e que a gente consiga realizar esses sonhos", concluiu.

Letícia e o marido Pedro — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A glicogenose é uma doença que afeta o metabolismo do glicogênio, uma substância que funciona como um "estoque de carboidratos", principalmente, no fígado.

Quando há uma necessidade maior de energia, como durante uma atividade física ou jejum prolongado, o organismo precisa fazer a degradação do glicogênio.

Letícia Ramos, de Uberaba, descobriu a glicogenose aos 2 anos de idade — Foto: Letícia Ramos/Arquivo

"Os portadores de glicogenose não têm essa capacidade por um defeito na enzima que degrada o glicogênio, ou seja, esse estoque não é mobilizado. Com isso, a doença pode afetar o fígado, os músculos e o intestino", explicou a endocrinologista e mestra em reabilitação Renata Liboni.

Segundo a médica, pessoas com glicogenose estão mais propensas a ter episódios de hipoglicemia, o que pode levar a convulsões e, em casos mais graves, à morte.

"Também estão mais propensos a inflamações respiratórias e, dependendo do grau, a alterações no crescimento, problemas no fígado, como cirrose e, até mesmo, o câncer no fígado", acrescentou Liboni.

A recomendação dos especialistas é que pacientes com glicogenose ou sintomas semelhantes não adotem dietas ou tratamento sem prescrição ou orientação médica.

Para ajudar os pacientes a controlar a glicemia, os médicos recomendam a ingestão do amido de milho, que evita o acúmulo do glicogênio no fígado.

"O amido de milho cru deve ser pesado em balança para um correto tratamento, evitando o excesso de ingestão de amido e obesidade desnecessária, e também evitando o tratamento insuficiente, não mantendo a glicemia em níveis normais", disse a gastrohepatologista e cirurgiã de transplantes hepáticos Eloiza Quintela.

Ainda conforme Quintela, a aderência ao tratamento é um grande desafio tanto para pacientes, como seus familiares ou cuidadores, porque exige cuidados rigorosos e muita disciplina.

"É uma doença que impõe mais restrições aos portadores do que o diabetes. Em razão do risco de hipoglicemia, as pessoas acometidas por essa enfermidade devem se submeter a dietas rigorosas de restrições de açúcar e realizar vários testes diários do nível de glicose sanguínea", finalizou.

articles.title: Acidente em Copacabana: polícia investiga causas | G1
articles.standfirst: Pelo menos três pessoas que seriam da mesma família foram atropeladas; idosa de 98 anos foi socorrida com estado de saúde grave. Uma das hipóteses investigadas é que a idosa de 80 anos que dirigia o carro confundiu pedais.
articles.summary: Uma das hipóteses investigadas é que a idosa de 80 anos que dirigia o carro confundiu pedais.
articles.body:
A Polícia Civil investiga o que causou o acidente que deixou seis feridos no início da noite desta quarta-feira (11) em Copacabana, depois que um carro invadiu uma calçada . Uma das hipóteses investigadas é que a idosa de 80 anos que dirigia o carro confundiu pedais e apertou o acelerador erroneamente. Também será investigado se ela sofreu um mal-súbito.

O carro atropelou três pessoas na calçada até parar dentro de uma loja na Rua Siqueira Campos, em Copacabana, na Zona Sul do Rio, no fim da tarde desta quarta-feira (11).

Uma idosa de 98 anos foi socorrida com estado de saúde grave. Um vídeo (veja acima; imagens fortes) mostra o momento do acidente.

A idosa que conduzia o carro e uma cuidadora de 42 anos que estava no carona também foram levadas pra o hospital. Elas estão entre os seis feridos no incidente. Uma pessoa que estava dentro da loja também se feriu.

Segundo relatos de testemunhas, a motorista saiu de uma garagem, atravessou a rua, invadiu a calçada e só parou depois de atingir o interior do estabelecimento.

Vídeo mostra momento de atropelamento em Copacabana — Foto: Reprodução

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado às 17h50 para uma ocorrência de colisão de veículo com outros.

Quatro feridos foram levados para o Hospital Miguel Couto por militares do Corpo de Bombeiros. Além da idosa, dois homens tinham ferimentos moderados e uma quarta vítima com ferimentos leves.

Uma quinta vítima foi socorrida pelo Samu e levada para o mesmo hospital e uma outra idosa, de 85 anos, foi levada para o Hospital São Lucas.

Uma faixa da Siqueira Campos foi liberada no trecho entre a Rua Barata Ribeiro e a Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana às 18h45.

Carro invade calçada e para dentro de loja em Copacabana; 6 feridos são levados para hospital — Foto: Reprodução

Carro invade calçada, atropela três pessoas e bate dentro de loja em Copacabana — Foto: Leandro Oliveira TV Globo

O acidente interditou trecho da Rua Siqueira Campos entre a Rua Barata Ribeiro e a Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana. Havia retenções na Rua Barata Ribeiro e na própria Siqueira Campos , a partir da Rua Silva Castro, por volta de 18h15. Equipes do Corpo de Bombeiros e da CET-Rio atuam no local.

Como alternativa, os motoristas que trafegam pela Rua Barata Ribeiro devem utilizar a Rua Hilário de Gouveia para acessar a Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana ou a Avenida Atlântica.

Atualização do trânsito em Copacabana às 18h30:

📍 Avenida Atlântica: vários trechos de trânsito lento em direção ao Leme. No sentido Ipanema, boas condições.

📍 Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana: retenções desde a Rua Souza Lima até a Rua Siqueira Campos.
