articles.title: Emocionada, adolescente que recebeu rim comemora alta hospitar | G1
articles.standfirst: Cáryta Micaelly, de 16 anos, deixou o hospital oito dias após receber a doação de um rim. Adolescente convive há 13 anos com doença que reduziu a capacidade do seu rim para 8%.
articles.summary: Cáryta Micaelly celebrou a alta após o transplante de rim que recuperou sua saúde, em uma trajetória marcada por 13 anos de espera e a esperança da doação de órgãos.
articles.body:
Um vídeo gravado pela mãe da rondoniense Cáryta Micaelly, de 16 anos, mostra a adolescente emocionada ao receber alta hospitalar depois do transplante de rim realizado em Campinas (SP). A menina que convive há cerca de 13 anos com uma doença renal hereditária recebeu uma nova chance de vida através da doação de órgãos.

"Eu vou acabar chorando. Eu passava a mão aqui [na clavícula], sentia um cano [cateter] de todo tamanho e agora eu não tenho nada", disse a jovem em um vídeo gravado pela mãe, Shirley Gomes, no Hospital da Unicamp.

Cáryta convive com uma doença renal policística hereditária desde os três anos de idade. Em setembro deste ano, a função renal caiu para 8%, o que levou os médicos a implantar um cateter para iniciar o tratamento de hemodiálise e incluí-la na fila de transplantes.

➡️ Os familiares acreditam que o órgão recebido pela adolescente pertencia a Miguel Meneses, de 14 anos, que morreu após um acidente de carro em São José dos Campos (SP). As duas famílias compararam datas, horários e características físicas e a partir disso acabaram se encontrando e compartilhando as próprias experiências em um momento de dor.

Goleiro Miguel Meneses, do sub-15 São José. — Foto: Reprodução/Assessoria do SJEC

➡️No Brasil, o processo de doação de órgãos é regulamentado por normas rígidas do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), que garantem o sigilo da identidade do doador e do receptor. Por isso, não há confirmação médica oficial de que rim recebido por Cáryta tenha sido doado por Miguel.

Cáryta passou por cirurgia para receber o novo rim na madrugada de sexta-feira, 30 de outubro. A liberação médica ocorreu oito dias após a cirurgia, realizada na madrugada de 30 de outubro. O rim começou a funcionar imediatamente após o implante, o que surpreendeu a equipe médica.

Apesar da alta, Cáryta e a família ainda não retornarão para Ji-Paraná (RO), cidade onde vivem. A adolescente permanecerá temporariamente em Monte Mor (SP) para fazer consultas e exames de acompanhamento. Ainda não há uma data definida para a volta definitiva a Rondônia.

Adolescente Cáryta Micaelly recebe alta após transplante de rim. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Família

articles.title: Justiça determina funcionamento de hemodiálise em hospital de Campina Grande após funcionários paralisarem atividades | G1
articles.standfirst: Providências deverão ser adotadas em 48 horas, sob pena de multa. Cerca de 100 pacientes foram afetados pela paralisação, que também suspendeu cirurgias pelo SUS.
articles.summary: Providências deverão ser adotadas em 48 horas, sob pena de multa. Cerca de 100 pacientes foram afetados pela paralisação, que também suspendeu cirurgias pelo SUS.
articles.body:
Justiça determina funcionament de hemodiálise após funcionários paralisarem atividades em hospital de Campina Grande — Foto: Reprodução/TV Cabo Branco

A 1ª Vara da Fazenda Pública de Campina Grande determinou o funcionamento contínuo e seguro do serviço de hemodiálise no Hospital Antônio Targino , nesta quinta-feira (12), após funcionários com salários atrasados paralisarem as atividades.

Na quarta-feira (11), o Ministério Público da Paraíba (MPPB) havia entrado com uma ação na Justiça para exigir a normalização do serviço de hemodiálise.

A paralisação dos funcionários também afetou a realização de cirurgias pelo SUS. Os trabalhadores suspenderam as atividades após completarem dois meses sem receber salários.

🔎 A hemodiálise é um tratamento essencial para pessoas com insuficiência renal. O procedimento filtra o sangue, retirando o excesso de líquidos e substâncias que os rins não conseguem eliminar. A interrupção das sessões pode trazer riscos à saúde dos pacientes.

O serviço de hemodiálise é gerenciado e operado pelo Instituto Social de Assistência à Saúde (ISAS). Na ação, o Ministério Público pede que, caso o instituto não tenha condições de garantir o atendimento com segurança e equipe suficiente em todos os turnos, a Prefeitura de Campina Grande assuma a responsabilidade pela assistência aos pacientes.

Caso o Isas não assegure o funcionamento contínuo do serviço de hemodiálise em condições regulares de segurança sanitária, o Município de Campina Grande deverá providenciar, em até 48 horas, a transferência regulada dos pacientes do SUS para outros serviços habilitados de terapia renal substitutiva.

Essa transferência tem como objetivo de garantir o custeio do tratamento e a não interrupção das sessões prescritas, até a regularização integral da unidade ou solução definitiva da rede assistencial.

Na decisão da Justiça, o magistrado estabelece que a Secretaria de Saúde do Município de Campina Grande deve fiscalizar, de forma efetiva e contínua, o cumprimento integral das obrigações impostas ao Isas, adotando as providências administrativas e contratuais cabíveis no prazo de 20 dias.

Conforme a determinação da Justiça, o serviço de homodiálise deve funcionar com médico nefrologista e equipe de enfermagem em número suficiente em todos os turnos de atendimento.

A determinação também estabelece que o serviço tem 48 horas para comprovar documentalmente as providências adotadas para cumprir a decisão judicial , sob pena de multa diária de R$ 5 mil, limitada inicialmente a R$ 200 mil.

Caso a multa tenha que ser paga, ela deve ser revertida ao Fundo de Direitos Difusos da Paraíba (FDD-PB), e de eventual responsabilização pessoal do gestor por crime de desobediência.

A investigação começou após denúncias de problemas no atendimento prestado a 89 pacientes renais crônicos. O quadro se agravou nesta quarta, quando o MP recebeu a informação de que o serviço paralisou devido ao atraso no pagamento dos funcionários.

De acordo com a apuração da TV Paraíba , os atendimentos estavam sendo realizados normalmente até esta terça-feira (10). Nesta quarta, no entanto, a falta de técnicos impediu a realização das sessões de hemodiálise.

Pacientes que chegaram ao hospital nas primeiras horas da manhã foram informados de que não poderiam fazer o procedimento e precisaram voltar para casa sem atendimento. Alguns vieram de outros municípios para realizar o tratamento.

Problemas já tinham sido identificados em outubro

Segundo o MP, os problemas estruturais e assistenciais já haviam sido identificados em outubro, durante uma inspeção da Gerência de Vigilância Sanitária de Campina Grande (Gevisa). Na época, os fiscais constataram a falta de um médico nefrologista como responsável técnico pelo serviço e buracos na escala médica em determinados dias da semana.

A fiscalização também descobriu que, por cerca de duas semanas, o tempo das sessões de hemodiálise foi reduzido de quatro para três horas por causa da falta de solução ácida. Houve também dias em que pacientes programados para o terceiro turno teriam ficado sem atendimento

Na Justiça, o Ministério Público exige a solução das pendências salariais, a normalização do estoque de insumos, a regularização da equipe profissional e a correção das falhas na estrutura física. A Promotoria pede ainda que o ISAS seja obrigado a apresentar e executar um plano de ação detalhado para adequar definitivamente o serviço às normas sanitárias.

O diretor executivo do Hospital Antônio Targino, Fabrício Targino, confirmou a paralisação dos funcionários e afirmou que a unidade depende de repasses das secretarias de Saúde do município e do estado para manter os pagamentos em dia.

Segundo ele, o hospital tem aproximadamente R$ 1,5 milhão a receber do município. O diretor afirmou ainda que há mais de R$ 700 mil em notas emitidas, mas que a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde informa que aguarda o repasse de recursos do Ministério da Saúde.

Fabrício disse que o hospital mantém contato diário com a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde para tentar regularizar os repasses e pagar os salários atrasados. Ele também afirmou que pretende dialogar com os funcionários para buscar uma solução e garantir a continuidade dos serviços, principalmente da hemodiálise.

O diretor, no entanto, não informou uma previsão para a retomada dos atendimentos. Segundo ele, a paralisação foi uma decisão dos funcionários, e não há como garantir quando o serviço será normalizado.

O Hospital Antônio Targino é uma unidade particular que também realiza atendimentos pelo SUS, com recursos provenientes de repasses públicos.

O g1 entrou em contato com as Secretarias de Saúde de Campina Grande, que, por meio de nota, informou que "tem conhecimento das dificuldades financeiras enfrentadas pelo hospital, que se encontra em processo de recuperação judicial". Afirmou também "que esse cenário não pode afetar os serviços contratualizados pelo Município para atender os pacientes do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) ".

A nota diz ainda que "o Município vem efetuando regularmente os pagamentos devidos à referida instituição, os quais são processados mensalmente. No período entre 1º de janeiro e 11 de novembro de 2026 a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde já realizou repasses superiores a R$ 8 milhões".

A secretaria disse ainda que encaminhou um ofício ao Ministério Público da Paraíba (MPPB), comunicando os fatos e apresentando documentos pertinentes à situação. Disse ainda que ainda nesta quarta-feira (11), "conforme planejamento e programação financeira da pasta, será realizado mais um repasse" ao hospital.

A reportagem também entrou em contato com a Secretaria de Saúde da Paraíba para solicitar esclarecimentos sobre os repasses ao hospital, mas, até a última atualização desta reportagem, não obteve retorno.

articles.title: She’s delivered 2,000 babies. The measles outbreak changed her mind about vaccines.
articles.summary: Traditional midwives like Roberta Devers could be key to increasing vaccination as outbreaks spread in rural communities such as those in Pennsylvania.
articles.body: This is part of The Vaccine Divide, a data investigation into America’s potential loss of its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble. When Roberta Devers, a midwife in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, did a prenatal check on an expectant mom this week, the woman — a member of the Amish community in her third trimester — had been sick with measles. Devers said she has cared for dozens of pregnant women infected with the virus since measles began spreading rapidly in the county in April. Lancaster County is largely rural, with sprawling family farms. “Every single day,” she said, “someone’s calling to ask what they do. They’re pregnant and they’ve gotten it, or their babies have gotten it.” Devers, 63, estimates she has delivered nearly 2,000 babies in her 38-year career. She has a degree in maternal and fetal health, but she is working as an unlicensed, traditional midwife in Pennsylvania, independent of the hospital systems and without physician oversight. State law bars traditional midwives from practicing medicine. Devers said she questioned immunizations as a young mother and never vaccinated her son. “There was as much information against vaccines as there was about the efficacy of vaccines,” she said. “It was difficult to know who to trust and who to believe.” Her experiences in Lancaster County’s outbreak have changed her mindset. “Numbers and books became people,” she said. “It was humanized by watching what was happening to the mothers I was serving.” In mid-October, the Pennsylvania Health Department alerted doctors about a rise in measles infections in pregnant women and newborns. As of Wednesday, state health officials had confirmed measles in 97 pregnant women. There’s no data, however, on how many miscarriages have occurred because of measles. Devers said one of her young mothers went into labor at 17 weeks, losing her baby. “There was no doubt in my mind that it was the measles,” she said. “Two weeks earlier, she had gotten the measles and then miscarried.” Midwives like Devers are the closest many pregnant women in the community come to mainstream medicine. Medical or vaccination clinics aren’t always easy to reach in rural areas, especially for Amish families who rely on horses and buggies for transportation. The families tend to rely heavily on health advice from midwives because they work with generations of women in the same families. Devers even offers a discount to her longtime clients: After nine babies have been delivered, the 10th is free. “We’re involved in the most intimate experience of their lives. We’re in their bedrooms. We have long conversations at the kitchen table about health,” Devers said. “We are their trusted practitioners.” Devers can give advice to isolate, minimizing spread of the highly contagious virus. She can explain the risks of measles infections during pregnancy, such as preterm birth and miscarriage. She can’t do the thing experts say is critical in curbing the outbreak: administer measles vaccines. “People ask me, ‘Do you have that vaccine in the car?’” she said. Many inquiries are from unvaccinated husbands, she said, wary of being exposed to measles at work and then bringing the virus home to their wives and children. “I have to say no. Midwives requested directly to the Health Department that we be allowed to carry this vaccine, and we were told no.” The Pennsylvania Health Department said in a statement that it “does not have the authority under current state law to allow traditional midwives to administer vaccines, nor does DOH regulate the practice of medicine in the Commonwealth.” Any change would need to come from the Legislature. There are opportunities for people to get the measles vaccine in Pennsylvania, and those shots can come from certified, licensed nurse midwives under state law. The Health Department said it has given nearly 11,000 measles-mumps-rubella vaccinations this year. A survey of Amish families in Lancaster County found that nearly half had home births in 2022. Those families have increasingly rejected routine childhood vaccinations. Less than a third — 30% — said they vaccinated their children in 2022, compared with 52% in 2014. A new NBC News/Stanford University data investigation reveals how far measles vaccination rates have plummeted not just among the Amish, but also nationwide. As of the start of the 2025-26 school year, 75% of U.S. counties and jurisdictions with measles-mumps-rubella vaccination data fell below the threshold needed for herd immunity for measles, up from 67% in 2024-25. Lancaster County is a prime example. Before the pandemic, the county’s MMR immunization rate was 95.5%, the level needed to prevent an outbreak. Last school year, just 87.6% of kindergartners in the county had received measles shots, NBC News data found. Some parents stopped getting routine childhood vaccinations in the 1990s and early 2000s, when misinformation about the safety of the shots began to catch fire. Those children are now old enough to become parents themselves, like Hannah Garman, 27, of Lancaster County. She’s due in early December with her third baby. “We weren’t raised with doctors when I was young, so I actually never got them,” Garman said, referring to vaccines. She is taking modest precautions to stay away from people who are sick, but she is largely relying on a good diet and her Christian faith to protect her from catching measles in the outbreak. As of Wednesday, 1,505 cases had been reported in Pennsylvania. More than a third are in Lancaster County. ‘Babies gasping for air’ Pregnant women are unable to get the measles vaccine because the shot contains a weakened but live version of the virus. Devers said the illness is affecting her clients in different ways. “Some are still on their feet doing their chores and working. Some are absolutely flattened by it.” Most children who catch measles will recover without problems. But some do develop complications and must be hospitalized. “Babies gasping for air, children needing oxygen and respiratory support, patients on ventilators. We see babies and children coming in with infections of organs within the abdomen, their liver, dehydration, babies that can’t take bottles,” said Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children’s Hospital in Hershey. “It’s honestly just been horrifying to watch.” Shirey has a 3-month-old son who is too young to get the measles shot. “I’m experiencing the outbreak as a doctor, but I’m also experiencing it as a dad, and I can’t protect my baby yet with a vaccine,” he said. “It’s scary.” Some children are developing brain inflammation called encephalitis, which may take months to resolve or be irreversible in some cases, Shirey said. Others are born with congenital measles. At least two babies in the state have died. How midwives could mitigate the spread Nearly all states have similar laws barring traditional midwives from giving vaccines without a doctor’s backing. New York recently declared a disaster emergency in response to its growing measles outbreak allowing unlicensed healthcare practitioners with a certain level of training or authorization, including some midwives, to give vaccines. It’s a step Katherine Wells, public health director for Lubbock, Texas, said she wishes she would have taken during last year’s outbreak among Mennonite communities in Gaines County. Using personal relationships between midwives and families would have been a good way to mitigate spread, she said. “During the emergency is not the time to be passing out your business card. You have to know those people,” Wells said. It’s critical in rural communities, she said, “especially in ones that are more religious and even more distrustful of government, to find individuals in that community who can speak to that community’s way of doing things.” Wells said she had the ability to train front desk staffers at the Public Health Department to deliver vaccines during the outbreak. “Theoretically, that order could have gone to midwives.” In Wisconsin, where a baby with measles has died, Korina Bauer, a certified nurse midwife in Shawano County, said she’s working with county Public Health Department colleagues to set up a measles vaccination clinic for her clients, many of whom are Amish. The state reports 551 measles cases as of Wednesday. Bauer is counseling two pregnant Amish women whose husbands were exposed to measles. “They’re concerned and want to know more about symptoms,” she said. “There is a lot of curiosity.” Devers said the Pennsylvania Health Department recently invited her and other midwives to an upcoming measles education webinar. “There’s a lot of home birth midwives in the state of Pennsylvania, and if they were given the opportunity to immunize, it would be another opportunity to quickly get people vaccinated,” she said. There are early signs that the spread may be slowing in Pennsylvania, with just 73 new cases reported this past week. That doesn’t mean the outbreak is over. November is the start of the traditional wedding season for many Amish families, timed to occur after the fall harvest. Weddings are usually quite large, easily topping 300 to 400 people. The pregnant Amish mom Devers visited this week said she has recovered from her measles infection and is feeling well enough to attend a wedding scheduled for Thursday. It appears the event will go on even though, Devers said, the bride has measles.

articles.title: Brandon Sklenar Opens Up About Experiencing Body Dysmorphia Since He Was 12
articles.summary: Actor Brandon Sklenar opens up about struggling with body dysmorphia from a young age and how the experience inspired his performance in the upcoming sports drama “Iron Jane.”
articles.body: Actor Brandon Sklenar is opening up about struggling with body dysmorphia from a young age and how the experience inspired his performance in the upcoming sports drama “Iron Jane.” The “1923” star, 36, explained his personal connection to his next project, which also stars Eiza González, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “Iron Jane” tells the story of a woman (González) who undergoes an intense transformation to become a competitive bodybuilder following a difficult childhood. Sklenar plays the former champion who guides her. Sklenar told the magazine he was intrigued by the film after previously working in an underground bodybuilding gym. “I personally was drawn to it because I grew up in northern New Jersey working in an underground bodybuilding gym. When I was 15, I was cleaning the floors, and by 18, I was a trainer, training everybody and running the whole gym,” he shared. “There was an MMA gym upstairs, and I would just train MMA all day and then train other people. I started doing martial arts when I was really little, like six.” Since he used to work and train in that world, he saw firsthand the posing, diets and steroids that are involved. Sklenar noted, “There is an element of ‘Iron Jane’ that really goes into body image and body dysmorphia, which is something that I just really feel needs to be talked about more, especially in this age of social media and fitness influencers.” “This is something I’ve struggled with, so we really wanted to translate that, and (director Lissette Feliciano) was really open to working with me on getting across (my character) Josh’s dysmorphia and what he goes through,” he added. “The Housemaid” star shared more details about his past struggles, revealing that they began when he was a child. “I was a little kid — short, chunky. I swam in a T-shirt and got made fun of. Then I had a growth spurt and became really lanky, and I got made fun of for that,” he recalled. “So I started training a lot and got obsessed with working out, like, ‘I’ll show them.’” The desire to prove them wrong turned into “a kind of obsession,” he said. “It becomes a very weird thing, where you see yourself completely differently than pretty much anybody else does, and usually in not a good way,” he explained. Sklenar said he is still tackling his body image issues. “Therapy helps for sure. If you look at me now as a 36-year-old man, you’d never guess it, but I still very much feel like that 12-year-old chunky kid — that sense of nothing is ever good enough,” he revealed. “You have to find a way to check your self-talk, because that’s really where it begins and ends — but it’s easier said than done.” He said that working on “Iron Jane” allowed him to confront some of his insecurities. He shared details of one scene that includes a full-body shot as he poses. “I’ve been pretty much naked in a film before, but it’s a whole different thing to literally be posing and have the camera panning up and down your body, detailing everything. When I was shooting that scene, I was so uncomfortable. Dealing with my issues, it was very challenging to work through that,” he pointed out. But, Sklenar said he reminded himself that González had to shoot that same type of scene repeatedly throughout filming. “Eiza trained her a** off, and she got in incredible shape for this film. I just have so much respect for her,” he praised. “Iron Jane,” which marks Sklenar’s first producer credit under his Vista Lane Pictures banner, is expected to debut at festivals next year.

articles.title: Trying Tourette's device tested by Lewis Capaldi was the best day of my life
articles.summary: Katie is one of many that say a device developed by researchers in Nottingham helped calm her symptoms.
articles.body:
When Katie was just a child, her tics were so relentless they left her bedridden with a sore throat for two weeks.

The now 15-year-old says living with Tourette's affected her ability to sleep, eat, and caused her to miss school.

But a wrist device developed by researchers in Nottingham helped her calm down in an "instant".

Katie recalled trying it on for the first time, and said: "It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life."

Tourette's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms usually starting in childhood.

Katie, from Hertfordshire, said she first started to experience symptoms aged seven.

She said: "It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, 'why are you doing that?'

"I used to make snorting sounds, but it was constant all the time, so I'd give myself a really bad sore throat and then be in bed for two weeks.

"I think I became quite sad a lot of the time."

Katie's mum Julia said it was "heartbreaking" to see her daughter struggling.

"You feel helpless. You feel you don't know where to turn really," she said.

It was not until she read about a wrist device - developed by the University of Nottingham - that Julia felt hopeful for her daughter.

She and Katie learned more about the device, and came to Nottingham to try it in December before it was available to buy.

Katie said when she turned it on for the first time, the effect was "instant" and she became "really calm".

"And I remember on the drive home, I just cried the whole way home because I was like, 'I want it now'," she said.

Katie was among the first people to use the Neupulse device.

It works by delivering electrical pulses to the median nerve at the wrist, which trials have shown can change the activity in the parts of the brain involved in movement control.

They found that rhythmic stimulation can reduce the frequency and intensity of tics.

In 2023, a clinical trial of 121 people in the UK found they experienced, on average, a reduction in tic frequency of 25% while using a prototype of the device.

That year, it was also tested by the singer Lewis Capaldi , who has Tourette's, prior to a gig in the city.

The university added Capaldi was impressed by the effects of Neupulse and was eager to try it out again in the future.

The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company Neurotherapuetics Ltd, which secured £1m in additional funding to commercialise the device.

According to the Tourettes Action charity , there are two versions of the device: Neupulse-C - which is available as a consumer wellness device - and Neupulse-M, which is intended to be marketed as a medical device specifically for the treatment of tics and Tourette's syndrome, but it has not yet received regulatory approval for this purpose.

Neupulse-M is still going through the regulatory approval process. It is hoped that if regulatory approval is obtained, the device will be considered for NHS use.

The charity added the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) had identified the technology as "promising", and had requested further evidence of its long-term benefits before making recommendations over NHS adoption.

The university said "thousands" of the devices had been sold so far.

Prof Stephen Jackson, who has led the research, said seeing the impact on users of the device had been "a dream come true", and hoped it would be available on the NHS "in the next year or so".

He said: "We are working diligently and as hard as we can to get regulatory approval for the Neupulse device as a treatment for Tourette's.

"It's been provisionally evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, but they were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval. That's something we're working towards."

In 2025, NICE added: "Our committee will meet again to appraise the clinical and cost effectiveness of the technology and publish new guidance."

According to Tourettes Action, more than 300,000 people in the UK have the condition, which is incurable.

Jackson said: "We've had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking.

"People saying they've been able to travel through the airport and travel on airplanes without ticking."

Among the users is 15-year-old Ollie, from Cheshire, who started making involuntary neck movements nearly two years ago.

"I just suddenly cracked my neck, and then about 48 hours after that, it was constant movements," he said. "It was incredibly sudden."

Ollie's dad, Alex, said daily tasks - including sleeping, eating and drinking - became "incredibly difficult", and said he and Ollie's mother were "at a loss... just watching our son deteriorate".

"There's a period of it where I didn't leave the house for about a month," Ollie said. "I didn't hang out with my mates.

"Reading and writing became really hard. I was out of school for six, seven months as I'm getting into GCSEs."

They heard about the device from the film I Swear , a drama based on the life of John Davidson, who is a Tourette's campaigner.

The family initially thought Ollie had Tourette's syndrome, but he was later diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) - a neurological condition that affects how the brain and nervous system work.

At that point, he said he came close to telling his parents "probably don't bother with this device", because he did not think it would work.

Alex said a few months ago, his son called them when he turned it on for the first time.

"You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped," he said.

Ollie said: "It's like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it's like getting part of your life back."

They both said the gadget had been "life-changing".

Emma McNally, CEO at Tourettes Action, said users she had spoken to had given the device "nothing but praise".

"Some people have said it's helped them to go to places that they've not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library.

"Other people have said it's helped them when they've been in a tic attack to help them come out of that to calm the tics and make them feel more relaxed," she added.

Mylo, 17, from Buckinghamshire, was involved in the clinical trial of the device in 2023 when he was 13.

He was recently given a device as a gift.

When he switched it on for the first time, he said he "instantaneously" felt the need to suppress his facial tics "going".

"As soon as it comes on, I can feel it," he said.

"I feel different... I feel new almost, which is strange. It's going to be such a big difference."

The device has recently been tested in early trials for people with Parkinson's to see if it can be used to reduce tremors.

Prof Jackson said the university was also looking to launch a UK-wide clinical trial to look at both anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

articles.title: La enfermedad que causa en torno a 2 millones de muertes por año: "Es especialmente peligrosa en personas con problemas de salud previos"
articles.standfirst: Hoy es el Día para recordar los síntomas y actuar a tiempo
articles.summary: Hoy es el Día para recordar los síntomas y actuar a tiempo
articles.body: Hay enfermedades que pueden pasar desapercibidas cuando hablamos de ellas y que, en realidad, son altamente dañinas para nosotros. Una de esas enfermedades es la neumonía que se lleva cada año en torno a 2 millones de vidas en el mundo. Un día como hoy, en el que se conmemora el Día Internaciona la Neumonía, es fundamental ser conscientes de los síntomas y de cómo puede afectarnos en realidad una enfermedad como esta que, además, es especialmente dañina para las personas que tienen problemas de salud previos, convirtiéndose en potencialmente mortal. Según los especialistas de Mayo Clinic, la neumonía es una infección que inflama los sacos de aire en un pulmón o en ambos. En los sacos de aire puede haber líquido o pus, el llamado material purulento, lo cual causa tos con flema o pus, fiebre, escalofríos y dificultad para respirar. Diversos organismos, como bacterias, virus y hongos, pueden causar neumonía. que puede variar en nivel de gravedad desde leve hasta mortal. Es más grave para los bebés y los niños pequeños, las personas mayores de 65 años y las personas con problemas de salud o sistemas inmunitarios debilitados. La mayoría de las neumonías se producen cuando se debilitan las defensas naturales del cuerpo, lo que permite que los gérmenes invadan y se multipliquen en los pulmones. Los signos y síntomas de la neumonía varían de leves a graves según factores como el tipo de germen que causa la infección, su edad y su estado de salud general, tal y como mencionan desde el blog especializado citado con anterioridad. Los signos y síntomas leves suelen ser similares a los de un resfriado o una gripe, pero duran más. Entre los síntomas que mencionan los expertos están el dolor en el pecho cuando respira o tose, la confusión o cambios en su percepción mental (en adultos de 65 años o más), la tos que con flema, la fatiga, la fiebre, la sudoración o los escalofríos con temblores, la temperatura corporal más baja de lo normal, las náuseas, los vómitos, la diarrea y la falta de aire. Además, es posible que los recién nacidos y los bebés no presenten signos de la infección; o bien que vomiten, tengan fiebre y tos, estén agitados o cansados y sin energía, o tengan dificultad para respirar y comer; es decir, que presenten síntomas similares a los de un adulto, según Mayo Clinic, blog especializado.

articles.title: Eduard Fernández, actor: “Cada uno tiene su droga estrella y la mía era el alcohol”
articles.standfirst: Esas fueron sus palabras en una entrevista concedida a Jordi Évole
articles.summary: Esas fueron sus palabras en una entrevista concedida a Jordi Évole
articles.body: Cuando pensamos en las adicciones, normalmente, solemos divagar hacia las más fuertes, o las situaciones más extremas que se nos ocurren. Sin embargo, no nos damos cuenta de que a día de hoy gran parte de las adicciones están normalizadas y tratadas como simples hábitos cotidianos. Sobre ello habló el actor Eduard Fernández en una entrevista concedida a Jordi Évole, en 'Lo de Évole', en la que comunicó la dura situación que ha vivido en relación al consumo de estupefacientes y otras drogas; mencionando que podía llegar a consumir desde las doce de la mañana. Pero una de las cosas que destaca es la problemática del alcohol, que en muchos casos, se convierte en una auténtica y dañina adicción sin que casi nos demos cuenta: “Cada uno tiene su droga estrella y la mía era el alcohol”. Aunque nos choque pensar en él como tal, el alcohol es considerado una droga legal, que además es psicoactiva y actúa como depresora del sistema nervioso central; por lo que ralentiza las funciones del cerebro y altera la forma en la que una persona piensa, siente y se comporta. Además de cómo funciona como droga, el alcohol, tiene una especial potencia para generar dependencia como consecuencia de un consumo continuado. Esta dependencia puede llegar a ser física o, incluso, psicológica. En el corto plazo, el alcohol, presenta unos efectos similares al de la disminución de reflejos, pérdida del equilibrio, alteración del lenguaje o menor capacidad en la toma de decisiones que puede resultar, en ciertos momentos y pese a no serlo, algo cómico. Sin embargo, cuando los niveles consumidos son mayores, deriva en intoxicación aguda y la pérdida de consciencia. El alcohol, pese a su nocividad, es una de las drogas más aceptadas socialmente, incluso siendo justificado por muchas personas el consumo en menores, incluso con el riesgo que esto supone para ellos. Esta normalización o cotidianización se sostiene en múltiples patas que hacen que se vea esta sustancia como un 'juego de niños'. Una de esas patas es la normalización cultural, ya que el alcohol está ligado a casi cualquier celebración, reunión o comida familiar. Incluso el ocio se relaciona con el consumo de este. Llega hasta tal punto que parece que beber es una norma y no hacerlo requiere de una justificación. Además, al ser legal se tiene la percepción de que no es tan malo, cuando hay muchas otras sustancias legales que son igualmente nocivas, como el tabaco. Por otro lado, está el sesgo de quienes creen que el alcohol solo es un problema para quienes sufren alcoholismo crónico, pero no para quienes consumen esta sustancia de forma habitual. Aunque solo bebas el fin de semana, si bebes mucho, es probable que acabes padeciendo problemas de salud graves en el futuro. Por último, es importante entender que muchas de las peores consecuencias del alcohol, ocurren dentro del hogar, donde los seres queridos sufren las consecuencias de este problema.

articles.title: Bridgend housing association worker stabbed in heart, inquest told
articles.summary: Clifford Foster, 61, has been charged with the murder of "most loving" mother Eleanor Barnfield, 47.
articles.body:
A woman was stabbed in the heart before crashing her car, an inquest has heard.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital on 19 October after being found by paramedics with injuries to her chest following the crash on Coity Road, in Bridgend.

An inquest opening at Pontypridd Coroner's Court on Thursday heard a provisional cause of death for the housing association worker had been given as "stab wound to the trunk involving the heart".

Clifford Foster, 61, has previously appeared in court charged with her murder .

The coroner's office told the hearing: "South Wales Police received a report of a road traffic collision in Bridgend on 19 October.

"The driver, Eleanor Barnfield, was found to have a stab wound to her chest by attending paramedics."

The inquest heard Eleanor was taken to the Princess of Wales Hospital in Bridgend, where she later died.

Coroner Rachel Knight said it was necessary to open an inquest, but it would be "suspended pending the criminal investigation".

Foster was charged following a "significant policing operation" around Ger-y-Nant, where he lived, and which is managed by the Valleys to Coast housing association, where Barnfield worked.

Ger-y-Nant is a sheltered housing and retirement complex of 13 flats, has non-resident management staff and accepts new residents aged 60 or over, according to an online profile.

Eleanor was described by her family as the "most loving" mother and "bravest person in the world".

In a tribute issued through police at the time of her death, they said: "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends.

Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, previously said the organisation was "devastated by the tragic death of our colleague".

"Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her.

"She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues.

articles.title: New prostate cancer screening guidelines include regular testing for most older men
articles.summary: As rates of advanced prostate cancer rise, the American Cancer Society is recommending that most men age 50 to 69 get a PSA blood test every other year.
articles.body: As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue a worrisome rise, the American Cancer Society is recommending that most men ages 50 to 69 get screened every other year. Those at higher risk, including Black men and others with close-family histories of the disease, should get the prostate-specific antigen blood test annually. Men ages 70 to 74 should discuss with healthcare providers whether the PSA test makes sense for them, based on their health and life expectancy, according to the ACS. The new guidelines, published Thursday in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, are the latest pendulum swing in screening standards for prostate cancer, which is the second-leading cause of cancer death among men, behind lung cancer. Dr. William L. Dahut, chief scientific officer of the ACS, said he hoped the new guidelines “would increase screening for men at average risk and ultimately lead to a decrease of men with metastatic disease or dying from the disease, while mitigating harm.” In the previous ACS guidelines, men ages 40 to 50 were advised to engage with their doctors in “shared decision-making” about PSA testing, as long as they had at least a decade of life expectancy. Repeat testing was based on a PSA-level threshold. Now, the ACS much more emphatically recommends that men should get the PSA test every other year after they hit age 50. Annual screening starting at age 45 is advised for two higher-risk groups: Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer and are likelier to die from it.Men who have fathers or brothers diagnosed under age 65 or who have multiple such relatives diagnosed at any age. The PSA blood test can help detect signs of prostate cancer earlier, when it’s generally more susceptible to treatment. There have long been concerns about PSA testing, because it can trigger unnecessary treatment with devastating side effects, and historically, research that it actually improved men’s survival chances was lacking. Rising cases of advanced prostate cancer The new guidelines were influenced in particular by a major randomized study of PSA testing in Europe that now has over two decades of follow-up and found that screening among middle-aged men did, indeed, lower prostate cancer deaths. Given those and other encouraging newer research findings, the authors of the updated ACS guidelines felt they could recommend the test as beneficial with greater confidence and be more specific about which groups should get tested and at what intervals. While the rate of death from prostate cancer fell by half over the past three decades, the decline has slowed overall and stabilized among men ages 55 to 69. The Food and Drug Administration approved the PSA test for cancer surveillance in 1986. Following broad use of the test for prostate cancer screening, late-stage prostate cancer diagnoses dropped by more than half and the death rate fell by 7% by the mid-1990s. But in the 2000s, various national health authorities became more concerned about overdiagnosis. So they narrowed the categories of men for whom they recommended screening. In 2012, the highly influential U.S. Preventive Services Task Force flatly recommended against PSA testing for men of any age. Diagnoses of late-stage disease subsequently began to creep up, leading to concern that lowered testing was a factor and, ultimately, to campaigns to once again broaden testing. An ACS study last year found that diagnoses of prostate cancer increased by about 3% annually from 2014 to 2021. Dahut, who was a co-author of the study, said the trend has continued in recent years. The study also found that over a decade of data, cases of metastatic prostate cancer increased by about 6% annually in men ages 55 and older. At its best, PSA testing can identify early-stage prostate cancer and lead to treatment — surgery and radiation is the standard of care — that stops it from spreading, improving men’s survival. Among men diagnosed with late-stage prostate cancer, only about a third live five more years. However, the PSA test often identifies cancers that won’t cause major sickness or death, at least not in the near term. In those cases, men would often be better off receiving ongoing monitoring rather than treatment. Many older men die with prostate cancer but not because of it. That’s a key reason the ACS and other health authorities don’t recommend the test for older men or others who most likely won’t live 10 more years. PSA testing can also produce false positives that lead to unnecessary treatment and anxiety. And the biopsy needed to diagnose prostate cancer comes with health risks. Crucially, surgery and treatment for prostate cancer can cause severe impacts, including sexual dysfunction, urinary incontinence and bowel problems. According to Dahut, recent improvements in medical practices have helped mitigate those effects. The previous ACS guidelines, issued in 2010, advised doctors to discuss with middle-aged men and younger seniors whether they’d like to take the PSA test. That more flexible dynamic left too many men forgoing the screening, ACS experts felt. The new guidelines urge doctors to more flatly recommend the test to that age group. Promisingly, doctors are better able to differentiate between prostate cancer cases that are serious enough to need immediate treatment and those that are better monitored over time. “Cancer still prompts a visceral, negative reaction in most people that for the most part is unwarranted in a lot of circumstances,” said Dr. Daniel George, a medical oncologist at Duke Health who specializes in urological cancers. George wasn’t involved with the new guidelines. “There are more cancer survivors in the United States than ever before in history,” he said. “That’s only going to increase. And that’s not because of overdiagnosis; that’s because of more effective therapies for these patients.” The change in guidelines could, in theory, have caught former President Joe Biden’s cancer earlier. Biden, 83, announced last year that he had aggressive metastatic prostate cancer that had spread to his bones. Biden had followed federal guidelines advising against PSA testing after age 70. Dahut said the revised ACS guidelines indicate the likelihood that many 70-something men can expect to live more than a decade longer, so prostate cancer treatment may help extend their lives. Biden said on social media this week that his “doctors continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment” and that cancer “hasn’t stopped me.” But he said that “sometimes it slows me down.” Accordingly, he said, he’ll be limiting his efforts to promote his upcoming memoir, which will be published Tuesday. In the book, Biden responds defiantly to accusations that he slow-walked cancer screening or hid his diagnosis, calling the suggestions “absurd.” “There isn’t anyone in this world with stage 4 cancer who doesn’t wish it had been caught sooner,” Biden writes.

articles.title: Don’t Ignore This 1 ‘Under-Appreciated’ Warning Sign of Heart Trouble, Doctor Warns
articles.summary: Shortness of breath can be a heart disease symptom, especially if accompanies leg swelling. Doctor explains when the warning sign should be checked out.
articles.body: Chest pain is a well-known heart disease warning sign, but there’s another symptom to watch for when it comes to cardiovascular trouble. It could show up gradually, disrupting everyday tasks, or even wake you up at night. The symptom is uncomfortable, yet might still be dismissed as something minor. It shouldn’t be, doctors say. Heart Health Tip of the Day: Don’t Ignore Shortness of Breath Also known as dyspnea, shortness of breath is a symptom to be concerned about, particularly if it’s triggered by simple everyday activities, warned Dr. Cedrek McFadden, a board-certified surgeon. “It is very under-appreciated,” McFadden said on TODAY. “Many people say, ‘I’m just out of shape right now.’ But these are people who may have gone from walking easily to now being winded from just taking the groceries in the house or even just avoiding stairs altogether.” Why It Matters Shortness of breath can happen when the heart isn’t working properly. It can be one of the symptoms of a heart attack, or it could indicate heart failure. Heart failure is when the heart is too weak to pump as it should or can’t fill up with enough blood, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute. If you find that you’re breathless to the point that you can’t finish sentences or wake up at night gasping for air, it’s an issue that should be checked out, especially if you also have swelling in the ankles, McFadden said. Swelling in the lower extremities can happen when blood flow slows due to a weaker heart and backs up in the leg veins, according to the National Library of Medicine. “If you have swelling with that shortness of breath, you’ve got to talk with your doctor as well. That could be that your heart is not working efficiently,” McFadden noted. How to Get Started Pay attention to how your body responds to everyday activities like climbing stairs or walking to the mailbox. Do you feel very out of breath or even have to stop midway and take a break? Is the sensation becoming progressively worse? Let your doctor know. “I find as a physician, one of the most helpful questions when somebody comes in and says they’re breathless, I say, think back: Could you do that earlier this summer or last summer, and now you can’t?” Dr. Sharonne Hayes, a cardiologist at the Mayo Clinic, previously told TODAY.com. If so, it may be time for a cardiac evaluation, she noted. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Ozempic and Zepbound users face 6 rebound risks after stopping, doctor warns
articles.summary: Thinking of quitting a GLP-1? A physician outlines six risks, from weight regain and muscle loss to worsening biomarkers and mental health consequences.
articles.body: While GLP-1 medications like Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound have reshaped weight management and diabetes control, research shows that many patients stop taking them within a year. Research has found that cycling off these medications can bring potential rebound risks, ranging from rapid weight regain to the loss of cardiovascular protection. Dr. Frank Dumont, internal medicine physician and executive medical director at Virta Health in San Francisco, spoke with Fox News Digital about why patients stop taking GLP-1s, the potential risks and how to maintain progress afterward. TYPE 2 DIABETES PATIENTS 21 TIMES MORE LIKELY TO ACHIEVE REMISSION WITH INTENSIVE LIFESTYLE CHANGES Why patients stop Some patients may stop taking GLP-1 medications because of medical concerns or side effects, while others prefer not to remain on long-term medication, Dumont said. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation and diarrhea. "Those types of things can become troublesome enough that people actually have a hard time eating enough food to get good nourishment," he told Fox News Digital. "Working with your physician to make a decision about whether it's right for you to stay on the medicine or not is important." Other serious side effects, like acute pancreatitis, would prompt immediate discontinuation of the drug. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS "We know that's fairly rare, but if the pancreas becomes involved, that is not a good thing," Dumont said. "It can be very serious. It can even be life-threatening." Certain GLP-1 medications carry a warning about thyroid tumors based on animal studies, though the risk in humans remains unknown. "When people take the GLP-1 medications, they lose weight, but they tend to lose both fat mass and lean muscle mass." These medications should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or a condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Dumont outlined six potential risks patients may face after stopping a GLP-1. No. 1: Return of hunger and cravings The most immediate side effect patients notice after stopping a GLP-1 is the return of intense cravings and a sharp spike in appetite, often referred to as "food noise," according to Dumont. Many patients assume they can treat GLP-1s like a short-term prescription, taking the drug to hit a target weight or blood sugar goal and then stopping, the doctor noted. However, major medical organizations, including the American Medical Association (AMA) and the Obesity Medicine Association, classify obesity as a chronic condition that typically requires ongoing management. "Unless you have significantly changed what you're doing in terms of the types of foods you're eating, it's likely you'll go back to the same foods you were eating before, and hunger and cravings will go up," Dumont said. No. 2: Weight regain It is typical for GLP-1 users to experience weight regain after quitting, according to Dumont. In the STEP 1 trial extension, participants regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year of stopping semaglutide and lifestyle interventions. WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF In the SURMOUNT-4 trial for tirzepatide, patients who were switched to a placebo after 36 weeks of treatment regained more than half the weight they had lost over the following year, even while receiving diet and exercise counseling. "That's just so devastating for people who felt like they'd finally found a solution that would work," Dumont said. No. 3: Change in biomarkers Biomarkers — which are measurable indicators of what’s happening inside the body, such as blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol levels — tend to improve while taking a GLP-1, which is beneficial for those with prediabetes or diabetes. When a GLP-1 is stopped, these markers can reverse if not countered with a change in diet, according to Dumont. Improvements in fatty liver disease may also fade after treatment stops, the doctor said. "We know that these medications can help to decrease some of that steatotic or fatty liver disease that occurs," he noted. "And when you go off the medicine, if you go back to eating the way you did before, those numbers have a tendency to worsen." No. 4: Worsening body composition Weight loss while taking GLP-1 medications can include a loss of muscle, raising concerns about body composition and long-term physical function, according to Dumont. "When people take the GLP-1 medications, they lose weight, but they tend to lose both fat mass and lean muscle mass," he told Fox News Digital. In a body-composition study of tirzepatide, about 25% of the weight lost was lean mass, which includes muscle and other nonfat tissue. The remaining 75% was fat. Dumont expressed concern that patients who regain weight after stopping treatment may not fully replace the muscle they lost. "So, there's a bit of a ratcheting-down effect if someone is on and off these medications, where they lose fat and muscle, stop the medicine, regain fat, go back on the medicine, and lose fat and muscle," he added. The doctor emphasized that preserving muscle is important for metabolism, injury prevention and everyday activities. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES No. 5: Mental health effects In addition to the physical consequences, Dumont noted that stopping a weight-loss drug can take a heavy toll on mental health. Many patients have spent years cycling through diets and programs without lasting success, often viewing GLP-1s as a final solution, according to the doctor. When the medication isn't right for them — adding to a history of past weight-loss setbacks — experiencing a "regression on all fronts" can be "really devastating from a mental health standpoint," Dumont said. "It can make you feel disheartened and like you don’t have the control you thought you did," he added. No. 6: Loss of health protection An observational study published in BMJ Medicine found that adults with type 2 diabetes who stopped GLP-1 treatment had a higher risk of major cardiovascular events than those who continued. Longer periods without treatment were associated with greater risk. Dumont noted that the stakes of stopping a GLP-1 go far beyond weight, pointing to the broader risk of losing metabolic benefits. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER While taking a GLP-1, lower inflammation and improved cholesterol and blood sugar levels help reduce the risk of major events like heart attacks and strokes, the doctor said. "But again, if you stop the medicine and you haven't changed the way that you eat, then all of those numbers can worsen … and that can then increase the risk of those bad things happening — things that can be devastating from a life quality standpoint, but also can shorten your life," he warned. Making your progress last Reaching metabolic goals and making lasting lifestyle changes may help patients maintain their progress after stopping a GLP-1, according to Dumont. "We actually have peer-reviewed published data demonstrating that you can indeed stop one of these medications when you reach your metabolic goals," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Virta-affiliated observational study examined selected patients with type 2 diabetes in a structured nutrition program, so the findings may not apply to all GLP-1 users. The doctor recommended adopting sustainable eating habits before stopping a GLP-1. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The GLP-1 is not the only solution," he said. "It needs to be coupled with ... a way of eating that's going to work for you for the long term that allows you to stop the medicine successfully if you need to." Dumont recommended working with the prescribing clinician on a plan for stopping treatment and monitoring weight and blood sugar afterward.

articles.title: ‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare
articles.summary: Israel’s military campaign and mass detentions collapse Palestinian healthcare in Gaza and the West Bank.
articles.body:
In the early hours of Thursday, Dr Rizq Abu Shuaira was on duty in the surgery department of the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza. An Israeli strike hit the hospital , killing at least six people, including Abu Shuaira and a child.

Zaher al-Waheidi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Health in Gaza, on Thursday called it “a horrific crime”, adding that Israel targeted the surgery department. He called Abu Shuaira’s killing a loss to the medical profession in the enclave that’s struggling to cope with the large-scale destruction of health facilities since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023.

“The world woke up to the crime of targeting the Nasser Medical Complex,” al-Waheidi said, adding that Abu Shuaira was “martyred while on duty providing services to patients”.

“He did not deserve to meet his demise while among the patients in the hospital corridors,” he said.

Israel has repeatedly targeted Gaza’s medical personnel and hospitals in the past three years, killing at least 1,725 medical workers. Of the enclave’s 37 hospitals, 20 are partially functioning while 17 others have been rendered nonoperational. Health authorities say 44 percent of essential medicines are out of stock as Israel has continued to block the supply of medicines into the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Gaza said it was the seventh attack on the hospital, which serves at least 500,000 people in southern Gaza.

“Of course, this targeting led to widespread destruction inside the surgery departments and operating rooms, and led to major damage in the outpatient clinics, the radiology department and the laboratory department,” al-Waheidi told Al Jazeera.

The Gaza Government Media Office stated that it holds Israel and the United States directly responsible for the strike on the hospital, noting that the victims included a 13-year-old child.

The media office has documented 793 Israeli attacks on healthcare services. A comprehensive report published last month by Insecurity Insight on ReliefWeb revealed that at least 3,508 attacks on healthcare across the occupied Palestinian territory were reported between October 2023 and September 2026. An overwhelming 95 percent of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces.

In Gaza during that period, 399 health workers were detained, including Dr Husam Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, who has spent more than 500 days in Israeli custody.

“The Israeli occupation did not and will not stop targeting the health system,” al-Waheidi said.

Despite the so-called ceasefire signed between Hamas and Israel in October 2025, the Israeli attacks have not stopped in Gaza.

Israel has also been accused of expanding its attacks on medical infrastructure in the occupied West Bank. A World Health Organization report (PDF) covering hostilities from January to August 2026 documented 124 distinct attacks on healthcare in the territory. The WHO data confirmed four deaths and 40 injuries.

A subsequent monthly report issued by the Independent Palestinian Doctors Association (IPDA) in October 2026 painted a harrowing picture of escalating field violence. During October 2026 alone, the IPDA documented 23 violations against the healthcare system in the West Bank. Specific flashpoints highlighted in the report included Salfit Government Hospital, which was stormed by Israeli forces twice on October 14 to confiscate surveillance camera recordings, while a nearby ambulance centre was also violently raided.

Eid Dwaikat, media director of the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, shared with Al Jazeera the suffocating operational environment. “The work of the Red Crescent teams is in a highly dangerous and complex field environment, amid the continuation of the siege, closure, and restrictions imposed on movement and access to the affected areas, which constitutes a direct threat to the safety of paramedics,” Dwaikat said.

The human cost of these delays is measured in lives lost. “Preventing teams from reaching the injured and detaining them reflects directly on delaying the provision of life-saving first aid … which multiplies the risk of death or the exacerbation of critical injuries due to not receiving medical care in a timely manner,” he added.

The crisis has been vastly exacerbated by the systemic imprisonment of Gaza’s doctors. Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) has highlighted the plight of 14 detained Palestinian doctors, including hospital directors and specialised surgeons held without formal charges.

“Holding doctors for nearly two years under what is called the ‘Unlawful Combatants Law’ without pressing any charge and without trial … of course is incorrect,” al-Waheidi, the Gaza Health Ministry spokesperson, said.

“If the Israeli authorities have any evidence, they should present it in a fair public trial. But detention without charge and refusing independent medical examination under security pretexts is an arbitrary deprivation.”

Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, was detained in 2024, and his case has become emblematic of the systemic abuse within Israeli detention facilities.

On Wednesday, the PHRI said it obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a weight loss of 14kg (31lb) in four months, a significant drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain. On Wednesday, the Israeli Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking his release and refused to allow an independent physician to examine him.

“In particular, we have documented and heard directly from the lawyer who visited Dr Husam Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital: severe beatings, loss of consciousness, and a feeling by Dr Abu Safia that if this continues unchecked, his life is in danger,” Tirza Leibowitz, executive director of PHRI, told Al Jazeera.

“The torture and abuse have risen to such a level that we draw conclusions about this being a policy that has been implemented by the Israeli Prison Service against Palestinian detainees,” she said.

Leibowitz pointed out the plight of some 10,000 Palestinians held in Israeli detention under various categories. “The situation is appalling, both in terms of the conditions in the prisons and the violence and daily abuses that they are suffering,” she said.

For the family of Abu Safia, the continued incarceration has been unbearable. Elias Abu Safia, his son, described the immense psychological toll of the prolonged separation.

“Unfortunately, we haven’t spoken with my father for the past 685 days. We only know about our father through the lawyer,” Elias told Al Jazeera. “We dream of being in touch with my father, to have a direct phone call with him. However, Israel is depriving us of having a direct conversation with my father.”

“The information that we are receiving about the health conditions of my father and how he is being arrested is very concerning. He doesn’t deserve to be treated that way inside or within the Israeli prisons,” Elias said.

articles.title: For alpha-gal patients, allergy drug could cut the severity of reactions to red meat
articles.summary: There’s emerging evidence that the allergy drug omalizumab may reduce severe allergic reactions for alpha-gal syndrome, a red meat allergy triggered by a tick bite.
articles.body: There’s emerging evidence that the allergy drug omalizumab may reduce severe allergic reactions for alpha-gal syndrome, a red meat allergy triggered by a tick bite. In a study presented Thursday at the annual meeting of the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, researchers found that 95% of participants using the drug experienced meaningful reductions in the frequency or severity of their allergic reactions. The study included 64 people with confirmed alpha-gal diagnoses who took omalizumab for an average of 23 months. The findings haven’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal. Alpha-gal syndrome is predominantly associated with the lone star tick. When the tick feeds on mammals like cows, deer, pigs and goats, it can pick up a sugar molecule in their blood called alpha gal. When the tick goes on to bite a human, it can transmit that sugar, which, in some people, can trigger an allergic reaction to red meat and, in some cases, gelatin and dairy products. The allergic reactions can range in severity, from hives to severe stomach pain to life-threatening anaphylaxis, among other symptoms. Because of that, doctors typically advise patients to avoid red meat and meat-based soups and gravies, as well as to consider avoiding gelatin or dairy. Omalizumab (brand name: Xolair) is already approved for people with severe food allergies, including peanut, egg and dairy allergies. It works by targeting immunoglobulin E (IgE), the antibody that drives allergic reactions, and removing it from the bloodstream. “If you have less IgE, it’s going to take a much higher dose of an allergen to trigger a reaction,” said Dr. Erin McGintee, an allergy and immunology specialist at ENT & Allergy Associates and Stony Brook Medicine tick-borne disease adviser. The drug isn’t a cure for food allergies, and people taking it still need to avoid the foods they are allergic to. Instead, it acts like a safety layer, reducing what could be a severe, life-threatening reaction to something more manageable if a person accidentally eats the allergy-causing food. Candice Matthis, 46, of Charlottesville, Virginia, was diagnosed with alpha-gal syndrome in 2019 after 12 years of symptoms. “I wasn’t aware of alpha gal at the time,” said Matthis, who later co-founded the nonprofit Alpha-Gal Foundation. “I never even asked, because it was just such an inconsistent reaction. I could eat steak or dairy and not have a reaction. A lot of people deal with that — they may have a reaction once and not the next time — so it’s hard to draw a correlation with this allergy.” Matthis, who wasn’t part of the new study, was prescribed omalizumab for other food allergies. She has been taking it for a year and said she has seen substantial improvement. “It’s definitely helped with my reactivity,” she said. “I accidentally drank milk at Starbucks. They put whole milk in my coffee instead of oat milk, and I took a big sip of it. My stomach hurt a little bit, but I didn’t have anaphylaxis.” Dr. Collette Tilly, an allergy and immunology fellow at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who led the study, said, “Our findings suggest that omalizumab may offer an important additional option for patients who continue to experience reactions.” McGintee, who wasn’t involved with the study, called the new data “really exciting and encouraging.” However, she cautioned against using omalizumab inappropriately, for example as a means of enabling alpha-gal patients to be able to eat red meat again. “This is a pharmaceutical product that’s not inexpensive,” she said. “The purpose of it is to keep people safe and prevent life-threatening allergic reactions. I think there’s kind of an important distinction there.” Eight people in the study were able to fully incorporate red meat into their diets again, but Tilly cautioned against interpreting this as evidence that omalizumab can lead to remission of alpha-gal syndrome. Some patients do experience naturally declining alpha-gal IgE levels over time, she said. “It remains unclear whether omalizumab increased reaction thresholds, facilitated reintroduction in patients whose sensitivity was already waning, or both,” she said. It wasn’t possible, Tilly said, to determine whether those eight individuals had truly regained tolerance to red meat, as to assess that they would need to continue eating red meat after the drug would need to be discontinued. This was not examined in the study. Dr. Supinda Bunyavanich, a professor in allergy and systems biology at Mount Sinai Health System in New York City, said the study’s findings were based on a retrospective analysis, and she called for a full clinical trial to be carried out with the drug. “If it were shown in a prospective trial to help reduce sensitivity [to red meat], I think that would go a long way in terms of improving the lives and the safety of people who live with alpha-gal syndrome,” Bunyavanich said. However, Tilly said an omalizumab trial would be ideal and is very much needed to identify which patients are likeliest to benefit, as well as the optimal treatment duration and dosing strategies. But persuading people to take part in such a study would be highly challenging. That’s because such a study would be likely to require deliberate food challenges in which the participants would be required to ingest red meat, and they would need to be monitored for many hours before they could be discharged. “They’d be committed to a full day in the clinic,” she said. In the meantime, McGintee suggested, omalizumab could best be used on a temporary basis in patients who have severe reactions, in which blood testing reveals very high levels of IgE antibodies against alpha gal. The need for new treatment options is particularly pressing, as cases of alpha-gal syndrome are on the rise in the U.S., driven by shifting patterns in the distribution of ticks. A study carried out this year by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that an estimated 24% of adults who live in five states where lone star ticks are prevalent had antibodies to alpha gal, suggesting that they had been bitten by ticks and exposed to the molecule at some point. McGintee and Bunyavanich described having witnessed increasing numbers of positive cases in their practices. “It used to be something that would be mostly seen by our colleagues who practice in the Southeast or South, but we are increasingly seeing it now,” Bunyavanich said. McGintee said one of the best things alpha-gal patients can do is take measures to avoid subsequent tick bites. “If a patient can avoid that, their allergy tends to get better over time anyway,” she said. Lone star ticks are most active in the late spring, early summer and early fall. “At those times, people should be using tick repellents both on their skin and on their clothing,” McGintee said. “They should be used anytime someone is putting themselves in a situation where they might have tick exposure, and that can be walking in the woods, mowing your lawn, going golfing or hiking, especially if you’re spending time in an area where small rodents and deer are also spending time.”

articles.title: ‘Mormon Wives’ Star Aspyn Ovard Shares Her Daughter Has Terminal Cancer
articles.summary: Aspyn Ovard shared that one of her three children has terminal cancer. Here’ what she shared of her sickness and the toll it took on her marriage to Parker Ferris.
articles.body: Influencer Aspyn Ovard shared that one of her children has been diagnosed with terminal cancer, speaking out in the Nov. 12 premiere of “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.” Ovard, who shares daughters Cove, 7, Lola, 5, and Elle, 2, with ex-husband Parker Ferris, did not specify which child was sick. “Everything happened so, just out of nowhere,” a crying Ovard said during a confessional interview for the Hulu show, which premiered Nov. 12. “One day she was OK, and then the next day she wasn’t.” “At the hospital, you’re like, ‘It has to be fine,’” she continued. “You can’t fathom that they’re actually going to tell you that your baby has cancer, and that it’s terminal. She could be gone in a month, we don’t know. I’ve been living like that for over three years, just having no idea.” Ovard and Ferris were high school sweethearts from Utah who married in 2015 when she was 19 and he was 20. In 2024, she filed for divorce on the same day she announced the birth of their youngest daughter. Ovard said her relationship with Ferris was in trouble before they learned about their child’s illness. “My marriage was nowhere near in a place to be able to make it through something like this,” she said in the Hulu show. “We weren’t even going to make it through before this happened.” “It was just so toxic and hard,” she added. “And through all of it, I feel like I still tried to take care of him because I know how hard he’s grieving.” A few months after she filed for divorce in 2024, Ovard downplayed the thought she’d ever tie the knot again. “I don’t think that I really believe in the concept of marriage at this point,” she said on the “Weekly Trash” podcast. “I would have a long-term partner if I met someone, and I feel like this is it. But to get legally married, I wouldn’t ever do again. It’s just too hard to separate.” “I think just legally, it’s just too much to it,” she added. “Even the concept of marriage, you just never know what life is going to throw at you so I think to make those vows, I don’t feel like I can really commit to that even if I loved someone so much.” Ovard has since shared that she’s in a relationship with a married couple, Bri Davis and Billy Davis.
